docs.text: IBM BOB PREMIUM PACKAGE FOR Z

docs.title: i. Modernization is indispensable to the enterprise IT agenda
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) introduces the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z curriculum for hands-on enablement. [5 min]

RECOMMENDED: CLIMBING THE AI MATURITY CURVE (LEVEL 3)

This course assumes you have completed the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve with IBM Bob Level 3 curriculum and that its concepts are familiar ground: the Agentic Sidebar and its modes, Bob Rules and custom configuration, and the context window and its economics. The discipline that carried through every stage of that course applies here as well — Bob does the building, while the developer stays in control. The material ahead builds directly upon those foundations and will reference them throughout.

IBM sellers and business partners know first-hand from client engagements that the most expensive mistakes in modernization planning are the ones that are never scoped or accounted for in the planning steps. Certain elements are easy to ignore, but carry great costs if overlooked:

  • Hidden assumptions baked into the legacy code
  • The need to run old and new systems side-by-side during transition
  • The true shape of the dependency tree
  • Data conversion and organizational readiness
  • The external interfaces that must keep working throughout

A useful discipline for sizing this work considers six dimensions of AI-assisted modernization estimation:

  1. Structural scope — what is physically in-scope?
  2. Semantic complexity — what behavior has to survive the change?
  3. Knowledge transparency — can the system explain itself? Searchable internal knowledge changes the economics of modernization, well beyond developer convenience.
  4. Integration and data surface — which boundaries must keep working? Modernization often fails at the edges: REST APIs, SOAP services, message queues and the like.
  5. Feedback readiness — how quickly do you learn that something has broken?
  6. Operational and governance constraints — what rules shape the work before it even begins?

Taken together, these dimensions resolve to a readiness test worth carrying into any client conversation. A codebase is well suited to AI-assisted assessment when intent is visible and boundaries are documented, when feedback is fast, and when changes can be sliced safely enough to verify. A codebase is poorly suited when the opposite holds true:

  • Internal frameworks lack documentation and real payloads have no examples
  • Contract tests and test data are missing
  • The local build is unreliable
  • Shared libraries have no clear owner
  • There is no safe slice to run

As you will see in Module 1 | Understanding the CICS Banking Sample Application, building a rigorous understanding of the legacy application is what moves an estate from ill-suited toward modernization-ready.

COBOL IN THE PRESENT DAY

Many organizations today continue to rely on business-critical applications that were written decades ago. These systems power core business processes and have earned their longevity through decades of dependable service. One of the most common programming languages found within these environments is COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language).

First introduced in 1959, COBOL was purpose-built for business data processing, and it remains one of the most widely deployed enterprise programming languages in the world. For more than sixty years, organizations have used COBOL to build systems that process vast volumes of financial and transactional data with exceptional reliability. Today, a significant portion of the world's business transactions continue to pass through COBOL applications running on IBM mainframes. Typical COBOL workloads include:

  • Banking and payment processing
  • Insurance policy administration
  • Government records systems
  • Airline reservation systems
  • Payroll processing
  • Retail and inventory management
  • Financial accounting applications

Despite their reliability, many present-day COBOL applications now face mounting modernization pressures: aging codebases that have evolved over decades; limited (or altogether absent) documentation; a shrinking pool of COBOL expertise in the labor market; difficulty integrating with modern systems; and growing demand for cloud-native architectures and modern user experiences. As a result, organizations increasingly seek ways to transform these applications while preserving the business logic that has been trusted for years — and that is the challenge IBM Bob was designed to address.

Those pressures take a recognizable shape on IBM Z. Mainframe applications are complex and mission-critical, and they often involve millions of lines of code, which calls for platform awareness and a deep understanding of IBM Z technologies. Four challenges recur in client conversations:

CHALLENGE REAL WORLD EXAMPLE Costs and complexity Millions of lines of code across thousands of programs. The result is a set of deeply interconnected programs that are expensive to maintain and evolve Scalability and agility Lengthy release cycles, heavy governance and low developer productivity slow innovation and extend time to value Skills A reduced talent pool and a reliance on scarce domain experts leave teams without application understanding Risk and reliability Modernization carries high operational risk. An unintended change can affect mission-critical workloads, compliance and business continuity

THE MARKET IS ALREADY MOVING

Gartner expects 90% of enterprise software engineers to use AI code assistants by 2028, up from less than 14% in early 2024.1 Kyndryl's 2025 survey of mainframe organizations found that 88% have implemented or plan to implement generative AI tools as part of their mainframe modernization efforts.2 For most mainframe clients, the principal challenge is accelerating application modernization in support of broader business transformation.

1 Gartner, Top Strategic Trends in Software Engineering for 2025 and Beyond, July 2025 2 Kyndryl, 2025 State of Mainframe Modernization Survey, September 2025

docs.title: ii. What is IBM Bob?
docs.text:
IBM Bob is an AI-powered modernization and software engineering partner that supports the entire software development lifecycle. Where a traditional code-completion tool is anchored to the moment of writing code, Bob is designed to support the lifecycle around it. Bob plans, executes, validates and governs multi-step tasks on a developer's behalf, which lets teams:

  • Understand existing applications and analyze their business logic
  • Generate technical documentation and architectural artifacts
  • Modernize legacy systems and build new features
  • Create automated tests and accelerate development workflows in general

Enterprises are entering a phase of AI-driven development in which tools do more than suggest or autocomplete code: they operate and coordinate across systems. Four requirements follow from that shift and each is built into how clients work with IBM Bob:

  • Support across the SDLC, from planning through development. The value appears when AI operates inside the existing delivery pipeline
  • Understanding of entire applications. Safe orchestration requires application-wide context, which file-level reasoning cannot provide
  • Governance, security and human oversight by design, so that policy and accountability are enforced as the work happens
  • Execution of multi-step workflows. Outcomes require orchestration, iteration and validation, and a single prompt rarely supplies all three

Bob operates directly within the development environment, allowing developers to work alongside AI while maintaining complete visibility into every stage of the process. Throughout this lab, Bob will help you understand, extend and refactor two CICS COBOL applications in place. You (the developer) remain in the decision seat for every consequential step along the way.

docs.title: iii. What the Premium Package for Z adds
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) delivers a client-facing overview of IBM Bob Premium Package for Z. [15 min]

IBM Bob Premium Package for Z (PPZ) adds deep mainframe expertise to Bob, so that large and complex IBM Z applications can be modernized accurately and efficiently. It is an extension for the Bob IDE and Bob Shell that uses structured workflows, automation and AI-driven insights to examine, restructure and document legacy mainframe code. It supports COBOL, PL/I, JCL, REXX and HLASM, along with the CICS, IMS, MQ and Db2 middleware those programs depend on. In this lab you will work in COBOL and CICS throughout.

What sets IBM Bob Premium Package for Z apart from other coding assistants in the marketplace today are four key value pillars:

PILLAR VALUE Modernization accelerator Mainframe expertise and application metadata are embedded in the workflows themselves, which scales end-to-end modernization, accelerates onboarding and reduces reliance on scarce expertise. Streamlined experience Code analytics are unified with multi-model intelligence to enable literate coding: developers express intent directly in code and receive context-aware changes in place. Enterprise-wide awareness Centralized mainframe code metadata can be shared across the enterprise, so the model reasons beyond file-level scope and gains consistency and accuracy. Secure, governed AI IBM Z domain expertise embeds platform-aware security controls and governance-aligned guidance into the workflows, for compliant and context-aware outcomes at scale.

Those pillars are delivered through a handful of concrete mechanisms (that this hands-on lab will also exercise):

MECHANISM WHAT IT DOES LAB SECTION Specialized modes Purpose-built AI personas for specific tasks. Z Architect plans and analyzes mainframe applications before any implementation; Z Code explains, generates, modifies and refactors mainframe code. Users can switch between modes without losing context. Module 1 runs in Z Architect; Modules 2 and 3 run in Z Code. Their presence in the mode selector is the visible proof that your entitlement is live Workflows Guided multi-step analyses with built-in prompts. Examples include Explain code, Generate data dictionary, Extract business rules and Generate refactored service program Module 1 opens with the Explain code workflow Skills Reusable instructions that make a task run the same way every time, such as impact-analysis, data-dictionary-management and COBOL code generation. Module 1 (impact analysis), Module 2 (code generation) and Module 3 (the data-dictionary skill in Bob's to-do list) Tools The actions Bob can take: read and write files, run commands, scan the application into a metadata database (scan_program) and query it. Module 3 scans GenApp before it analyzes a single program Rules and AGENTS.md Repo-level files that set standards and guardrails for AI behavior, so outcomes are governed by default and predictable across teams. Registration and setup creates .bob/rules/file-organisation.md zContext Purpose-built IBM retrieval (RAG) that enriches the model with curated Z knowledge (languages, middleware, patterns and code samples) with no setup on your part Module 3's to-do list includes the step Assess Z Context needs and call z_context_tool

WHY DO DATA DICTIONARIES MATTER?

Mainframe variable names are terse, and a model that infers meaning from an abbreviation alone will guess. An enterprise-specific data dictionary gives Bob authoritative business context instead. In one documented example, a program's VO-FILE was explained as a voucher/order transaction file without a dictionary; with one, Bob correctly described the program as a flight-management routine that reads flight records for pilot statistics. The same context improves documentation, rule extraction and explanations while reducing hallucinations. You will see the data-dictionary-management skill appear in Bob's plan during Module 3.

Beyond the scope of this lab, the package also exposes enterprise-scale application metadata for architecture-aware analysis across hundreds of programs, and runtime awareness that captures execution paths and frequency patterns for production-aligned impact analysis.

docs.title: iv. How a prompt becomes a governed workflow
docs.text:
Any time that a user sends a prompt to Bob— such as "Create a new COBOL program that does X using my coding standards" —the Premium Package for Z works through four stages before it answers:

  1. Intent analysis and mode selection — Bob interprets the request and confirms the mode best suited to it
  2. Governance — Bob selects the applicable skills and the rules (or AGENTS.md) that constrain how the work is done
  3. Execution — Bob selects its tools: scanning the application and querying the resulting metadata, retrieving variables, and reading and editing files
  4. Reason and response — Bob synthesizes the results and reports back, with every file change presented as a diff for your approval

You will witness this deterministic workflow in action within the hands-on work ahead. In Module 1, Bob recognizes an impact-analysis request, loads the corresponding skill, and drafts a to-do list before reading the copybook. In Module 3, Bob's first to-do list runs according to the same pattern: it confirms the metadata database and scans the application; invokes the data-dictionary skill and assesses Z Context needs; and only then does Bob read the three programs it was asked about.

docs.title: v. The environment: two CICS applications
docs.text:
This lab works against two sample applications, each containing a small (but nevertheless realistic) CICS system of the kind found in banking and insurance estates.

The CICS Banking Sample Application (CBSA) is the subject of Modules 1 and 2. It is an enterprise-grade z/OS reference application that simulates core retail banking operations: customer onboarding and account management, together with deposits, withdrawals and fund transfers. It is built on IBM CICS Transaction Server for z/OS, Db2 for z/OS and VSAM, with a clear separation between its presentation, business service and data layers.

ARTIFACT ROLE IN THE APPLICATION 29 COBOL programs under cobol_src Presentation drivers, business logic services, an asynchronous credit bureau simulation and utilities 9 BMS maps under bms_src The 3270 screen layouts, including the main menu map BNK1MAI Copybooks under cobol_copy Shared record layouts and screen definitions, such as BANKMAP.cpy and CUSTOMER.cpy BNKMENU The entry point (transaction OMEN) that routes users to each screen driver BANKDATA The batch utility that generates the application's data INQCUST The customer inquiry service that five other programs call CUSTOMER (VSAM KSDS) and ACCOUNT, PROCTRAN, CONTROL (Db2) The persistence layer

GenApp, the CICS general insurance sample application published by the CICS development team, is the subject of Module 3. Its policy programs (LGAPDB01, LGUPDB01 and LGDPDB01) sit in the middle of a three-tier LINK chain that runs from the 3270 screen programs, through a business-logic tier, down to Db2 and VSAM. They share the LGCMAREA copybook as their COMMAREA contract and the LGPOLICY copybook for policy-specific definitions. Each of them validates requests in its own code, which is the duplication that Module 3 consolidates into a single service.

WHAT IS CICS?

CICS (Customer Information Control System) is IBM's transaction processing middleware on z/OS. A transaction starts a program; programs hand work to one another with EXEC CICS LINK and exchange data through a COMMAREA (communication area), a shared record whose layout lives in a copybook. Screens are defined as BMS (Basic Mapping Support) maps, which exist in two forms that must stay in sync: a physical map that CICS renders and a symbolic map that programs reference through a copybook. Data lives in VSAM files (a KSDS is a key-sequenced data set) and in Db2 tables, and a program abends with a four-character code such as ASRA when it fails. Every one of these terms appears in the modules ahead.

Both applications are intentionally small. They nonetheless contain many of the same programming concepts found within the real-world COBOL systems of banks, insurers, governments and financial institutions. Working against a believable codebase from start to finish, rather than a series of disconnected snippets, lets you watch Bob operate the way it would inside a client's modernization initiative.

docs.title: vi. Lab objectives
docs.text:
TO EFFECTIVELY MODERNIZE, YOU MUST FIRST UNDERSTAND A CLIENT'S ESTATE

Modernization projects frequently involve millions of lines of legacy code and decades of accumulated business logic. Rewriting that code is seldom the hardest part of the initiative. The far greater difficulty lies in understanding four things: what the application does, why it behaves that way, which business rules must be preserved, and how changes can be introduced safely. In the era of AI-generated code this understanding gains even greater significance. The developer's day shifts away from authorship and toward steering, constraining, verifying, and cleaning up what an agent produces. Judgment, in other words, becomes the scarce resource.

Enterprise mainframe environments add a difficulty of their own. They are vast and highly interconnected, with tens of thousands of tightly coupled artifacts and poorly defined boundaries, which makes the impact of any change hard to assess. Establishing clear application and solution boundaries is the first step toward scoping and modernizing these systems safely, and it is the reason this lab insists on understanding before change. Module 1 traces the potential impact from any changes to a single field before even touching a line of code. Module 3 documents the business rules and maps the dependencies across two full reports before any snippets of code are adjusted.

IBM Bob helps accelerate each of these activities, from application understanding and architecture discovery to code transformation, automated testing and documentation generation. All the while, the developer stays in control of the process.

This lab follows a realistic workflow for understanding and changing a mainframe application. You will use the Premium Package for Z to perform the same activities that teams undertake during modernization initiatives, organized across three modules that progress from analysis to change.

CHAPTER TOPIC WHAT YOU'LL TAKE AWAY Setup for IBMers IBM REGULAR EMPLOYEES ONLY. Register internally, request the Premium Package for Z entitlement through the w3 add-ons portal, install the extension and retrieve the CBSA source files with Bob A Bob IDE with the Z Code and Z Architect modes live, a workspace holding CBSA and the workspace rules Bob will follow Setup for Business Partners BUSINESS PARTNERS ONLY. Request the entitlement through IBM Technology Zone, bind the IDE to it and complete the same workspace setup The same validated environment, with no IBM intranet access required 1. Analyze ALL AUDIENCES. Explain a program with the Explain code workflow, document the CBSA architecture in Z Architect mode and trace the full impact of shrinking one copybook field Application understanding produced in minutes, with an impact report that separates true dependencies from look-alike fields 2. Build ALL AUDIENCES. Ask Bob for a plan to add customer search by email, review it, have Bob implement the COBOL and verify its syntax The plan-first habit, and a generated program that follows the conventions of the surrounding suite 3. Refactor ALL AUDIENCES. Identify GenApp's duplicated validation rules, map their dependencies, extract them into a shared LGPOLVAL service and wire the callers to it A monolith refactored in place, with every rule traced to its source and every change approved as a diff

docs.title: vii. Lab prerequisites
docs.text:
The hands-on work ahead assumes you have completed the core curriculum of the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve L3 course, or that you hold equivalent familiarity with the Bob IDE and the Agentic Sidebar as well as Rules and AGENTS.md. Your environment begins as a fresh workspace: nothing from the Galaxium Travels project carries over, and Bob retrieves the mainframe source files for you with a sparse git clone, so you will not work with Git directly.

What you do need:

REQUIREMENTS

  • IBM Bob installed and authenticated: the Registration and setup chapter has two versions (for IBM regular employees and IBM business partners)
  • Your IBMid credentials are at hand (IBM regular employees sign in with their w3id)
  • IBM regular employees: access to the w3 add-ons portal to request the Premium Package for Z entitlement. Approval is manual and takes 24 to 48 hours, so request it before the day you plan to run the lab
  • Business Partners: access to IBM Technology Zone to request the Premium Package for Z entitlement
  • Internet access to github.com, where both sample applications are hosted
  • A local folder is available to serve as your Bob project workspace

No additional downloads or staged files are required before you begin.

BUSINESS PARTNERS

Business Partners obtain their entitlement through IBM Technology Zone and follow their own Setup page, Business Partners | Registration and setup. That route is fully self-contained and requires neither the w3 add-ons portal nor an IBM intranet connection.

A WORD ON TOKEN BUDGETS

Every module ends with a reminder to watch your Bob token budget. Mainframe applications involve large and interconnected codebases, so the prompts in this lab consume more than a comparable task on a small project. Finish each module's prompts before you experiment with the optional variations.

docs.text:

docs.text: GETTING STARTED

docs.title: i. Before you begin
docs.text:
These instructions apply to IBM regular employees. If you are an IBM Business Partner, switch to Business Partners | Registration and setup, where the Premium Package for Z entitlement comes through IBM Technology Zone.

Before diving into the hands-on modules, complete the following registration and setup steps to prepare your machine with an authenticated IBM Bob account entitled to the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z (PPZ), along with a local copy of the CBSA sample banking application that the first two hands-on modules build upon. The work proceeds in six stages:

  • Register for IBM Bob through the Internal registration route (if you have not already done so) and authenticate the Bob IDE on your local machine
  • Request the Premium Package for Z entitlement through the w3 add-ons portal, then confirm it has landed in your Bob account
  • Install the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z extension and its companions from the Extensions view, plus the Draw.io Integration extension used for diagramming
  • Create a fresh project workspace
  • Retrieve the CBSA application source files (COBOL programs, copybooks and BMS screen maps) with Bob in Agent mode
  • Establish the workspace rules that govern where Bob files its documents, tools and diagrams throughout the lab

docs.title: ii. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure that you have each of the following in hand before starting; most setup stalls trace back to one of these.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN

  • Valid w3id credentials
  • Administrative rights to install software on your local machine
  • Internet access to github.com — the lab files are retrieved from a public repository
  • Roughly 24 to 48 hours of lead time: Premium Package entitlements are approved manually, and no approval email is sent

THIS LAB REQUIRES THE PREMIUM PACKAGE FOR Z

Without the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z (PPZ) entitlement, IBM Bob can still open and read mainframe code, though the Z Code and Z Architect modes and the specifically-trained capabilities that the package provides will be missing. If neither mode appears in your Agentic Sidebar by the end of this chapter, the entitlement has not been linked to your Bob account.

ALREADY HAVE IBM BOB?

If the Bob IDE is already installed and authenticated against the IBM internal Bob instance, skip section iii and jump ahead to section iv. The Premium Package request in section iv assumes that this onboarding is complete.

docs.title: iii. Internal registration
docs.text:
The Internal registration route is the appropriate one for IBM regular employees. It grants a general-purpose IBM Bob account tied to your w3id — the account that the Premium Package for Z entitlement is attached to in section iv.

  1. Begin at the Bob Enterprise Sales Assets page on IBM Technology Zone.

    Once there, click Technical Resources in the left sidebar.

  1. Click See it under the "Internal Bob Sign Up" tile.

  1. You will be redirected to a sign-up form. Enter all of the requested information and press Submit.

  1. Review your responses if you like, then confirm by clicking Submit once more in the pop-up window.

    There will be a "Thank you" pop-up that appears afterward — you can simply dismiss it.

  1. After submission, you will receive a confirmation email.

  1. At this point you will need to wait. Approval typically takes at least 24 hours (sometimes up to 48 hours).

    Once approved, you will receive an email — follow the Download Bob hyperlink within it.

  1. The Download Bob link opens a Box folder containing download links for various operating systems. Identify the version appropriate for your machine's operating system and select it.

  1. Click the appropriate file within the folder.

  1. Click Download.

  1. Review the License Agreement. If you agree to its terms and conditions, toggle I accept the agreement and click Next.

  1. Continue following the prompts of the automated installer.

    Review the instructions on each Setup page to configure Bob to your liking, and press Next to proceed.

  1. Installation should take roughly 2–5 minutes.

  1. A completion pop-up appears.

    Tick Launch IBM Bob (if it is not already checked) and press Finish.

  1. The IBM Bob IDE opens. Click Log in to Bob from the panel displayed within your interface.

  1. When prompted The extension IBM Bob wants to sign in using Bob, click Allow to launch a web browser for authentication.

    Log in via the browser using your IBMid and password (those which are linked to the IBM Bob account you registered for in the previous steps.)

  1. A few additional prompts may arise before authentication can complete:

    • If asked "Do you want to allow this website to open IBM Bob?", click Yes
    • Wait until the web browser refreshes to read Authentication Successful! before closing the browser window
    • Return to the Bob IDE, which has now been successfully authenticated and connected to the IBM Bob service

docs.title: iv. Request the Premium Package for Z entitlement
docs.text:
IBMer ("Internal" route) requests for IBM Bob Premium Packages are made separately from the requests for a general-purpose IBM Bob account. In other words: requesting an IBM Bob account (such as you completed earlier) does not carry entitlements for any Premium Packages (such as PPZ). A separate reservation request must be filed for such entitlements, which the following steps will guide you through.

  1. Navigate to the IBM Bob Premium Packages sign-up page. This is the IBM internal (w3) registration portal where IBMers request access to IBM Bob Premium Package add-ons.

    URL: https://w3.ibm.com/w3publisher/bob/addons

  1. Enter your Name and IBM email address (@ibm.com) in the form fields, then click SUBMIT. Note the reminder at the bottom of the page: you must already be onboarded to the IBM internal Bob instance (section iii) before you can sign up for a Premium Package.

  1. A "Thank You — Your form has been submitted" confirmation dialog appears over the page. Click Ok to dismiss it.

  1. Check your IBM email inbox. You will receive an automated confirmation from w3Notifications that your sign-up request has been received. The entitlement itself is granted separately, after a manual review, without an email notice.

    WAIT TIME FOR APPROVAL

    Approval typically takes 24 to 48 hours, and no follow-up email is sent when it lands. Confirm the entitlement from inside the Bob IDE, as described in the next three steps.

  1. After the waiting period, open the Bob IDE. If the Agentic Sidebar isn't already open, expand it by clicking the small Bob icon at the top-center of the screen (next to the search bar). No folder is open yet; you will create and open your working folder in section vii.

  1. Open Bob Settings by clicking the gear icon within the Agentic Sidebar.

  1. If the entitlement has been granted, IBM Bob Premium Package for Z appears in the Add-ons list. No verification email is sent, so this list is the place to check.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: NO ENTITLEMENT AFTER 24+ HOURS

    Some users have reported that the entitlement has not appeared even after waiting 24+ hours. If you experience this, request help in the #bob-and-friends Slack channel.

docs.title: v. Install the Premium Package for Z extension
docs.text:
With the entitlement in place, the next stage installs the extension that delivers it inside the Bob IDE. The Premium Package arrives through the Bob IDE's own Extensions view and brings three companion extensions with it.

  1. Click the Extensions icon in the left Activity Bar (the square icon), or press Ctrl+Shift+X. This opens the Extensions Marketplace panel where you can search for and install the extensions required for this lab.

  1. The Extensions panel opens in the left sidebar, with the Search Extensions in Marketplace search bar at the top.

  1. In the search bar, type the following. The top result should be IBM Bob Premium Package for Z by IBM. Several similar-named extensions appear below it — make sure you select the correct one.

    Premium Package For Z

  1. Click the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z result to open its detail page. Verify that the publisher is IBM and that the version is 3.0.0 or higher, which this lab requires. The detail page confirms this is the correct extension before you commit to installing it.

  1. Click the Install button on the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z detail page.

  1. Click the Clear Extensions Search Results icon (next to the search box). Clearing the search filter resets the Extensions view so you can see your installed extensions and verify that the package components were properly added.

    You may receive a pop-up window prompting you to restart after downloading the extension. If so, click the restart button to allow Bob to refresh.

  1. Under the INSTALLED section of the Extensions sidebar, verify that four extensions have been installed as part of the package:

    EXTENSION PUBLISHER PURPOSE IBM Bob Premium Package for Z IBM Mainframe-specific AI agents, modes and workflows IBM Z Open Editor IBM Language support and syntax highlighting for COBOL, PL/I, HLASM, REXX and JCL Mermaid MermaidChart Renders architecture and flow diagrams directly within the editor Zowe Explorer Zowe Interaction with z/OS datasets, Unix System Services (USS) files and jobs

    These companion extensions work together to provide complete mainframe development and diagramming capabilities within IBM Bob.

  1. Upon completing the installation, multiple welcome tabs open — for example, Welcome to IBM Bob Premium Package for Z in the main editor area. This welcome page outlines getting-started steps, key commands such as creating an AGENTS.md file using /init, and the available skills and workflows. Close all of these welcome tabs.

  1. Open the Mode selector drop-down in the bottom panel of the Agentic Sidebar (the mode pill next to the prompt area). A Bob Mode is a named persona with a specific role, tool access and behavioral constraints. Alongside the default Agent, Plan and Ask modes, two new specialized mainframe modes now appear:

    • Z Code: designed for implementing, refactoring and explaining mainframe code (such as COBOL, PL/I and JCL)
    • Z Architect: tailored for high-level application analysis, architecture mapping and program relationship discovery across mainframe assets

    The remainder of the lab depends on these two modes. If the entitlement was granted and the extension installed, they populate automatically.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: THE Z MODES ARE MISSING

    If you submitted the w3 form and installed the extension but these modes still don't appear, there was an issue with your entitlement. Request support in the #bob-and-friends Slack channel before continuing.

docs.title: vi. Install the Draw.io Integration extension
docs.text:
One additional diagramming extension is required for the lab.

  1. Click the Extensions icon on the left Activity Bar to return to the marketplace. The Extensions panel re-opens with the search input ready at the top.

  1. In the search box, filter on the following title:

    Draw.io Integration
    • In the search results list below, locate Draw.io Integration by hediet
    • Click the blue Install icon to the right of the entry to initiate the extension installation for your Bob IDE environment

  1. A confirmation dialog titled "Do you trust the publisher 'hediet'?" appears. Click Trust Publisher & Install to authorize the installation of the third-party extension into IBM Bob.

  1. Click Clear Extensions Search Results (the X icon in the Extensions search bar) to dismiss the search and return to the full Extensions list view.

  1. The Extensions panel now shows Draw.io Integration (by hediet) in the INSTALLED list alongside the other extensions you added earlier: IBM Bob Premium Package for Z, IBM Z Open Editor, Mermaid and Zowe Explorer. This confirms that all required extensions are in place.

docs.title: vii. Create the project workspace
docs.text:
Bob and the other extensions need a workspace folder to operate in. You will create a dedicated, empty folder for the lab and open it as the root of your project.

  1. Click the Explorer icon (the page icon at the top of the Activity Bar on the far left) to switch from the Extensions view to the File Explorer view.

    • The panel shows NO FOLDER OPENED, since the Bob IDE does not yet have a workspace folder set.
    • Click the Open Folder button to open a system file-picker dialog.
    • The Agentic Sidebar (on the right) should be visible and active.

  1. The file-picker dialog opens.

    Create a dedicated folder for your lab work by clicking the New folder button.

  1. A new folder appears in the file-picker with its name field open for editing.

    • Type a memorable name for your lab workspace: the example shown uses Bob PPZ L3
    • Hit Enter to confirm the name

  1. With the Bob PPZ L3 folder created and selected in the file-picker, click Select Folder to open it as your workspace. This tells the Bob IDE to treat this folder as the root of your project for the rest of the lab.

  1. The Bob IDE opens the Bob PPZ L3 workspace and the installed extensions automatically display their welcome tabs again: Welcome to IBM Z Open Editor in IBM Bob and Welcome to IBM Bob Premium Package for Z. Close both welcome tabs by clicking the X button on each tab.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: LOCKED IN RESTRICTED MODE

    When opening a new directory, the Bob IDE may automatically enable Restricted Mode, which locks out extensions and executables until such restrictions are lifted. If a blue Restricted Mode shield icon is showing in the bottom-left corner of the IDE:

    • Click the Restricted Mode button to pull open the configuration screen

docs.title: viii. Retrieve the CBSA lab files
docs.text:
The first two modules of this courseware work against the same application: CBSA, the CICS Banking Sample Application. Its COBOL programs, copybooks and BMS screen maps live in a public GitHub repository. You will have Bob retrieve the one sub-directory the lab needs, which spares you from cloning the repository by hand.

  1. Click the mode selector to open the Modes picker and select Agent mode. In Agent mode Bob can read, write and execute actions autonomously within your workspace — the right choice for pulling down the lab files in the next step.

    Notice again that Z Code and Z Architect appear in the list. These are the two custom modes added by the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z extension; the lab depends on them from the first module onward.

    TROUBLESHOOTING: THE Z MODES ARE MISSING

    If the extension is installed but these two modes do not appear in the list, there is an issue with your entitlement. Return to section iv and confirm the entitlement before continuing; IBM regular employees can also request support in the #bob-and-friends Slack channel.

  1. With Bob in Agent mode, paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar and press Enter (or click the send button) to submit it:

    Retrieve the sub-directory named "src/base" in the CBSA directory from the GitHub repository https://github.com/ovallod/Bob4z-a-thon.git and place it in the current workspace folder. Then remove any temporary working directory you would have created.

    This instruction tells Bob to clone only the src/base subdirectory from the CBSA repository (https://github.com/ovallod/Bob4z-a-thon.git) into your workspace folder, then clean up any temporary working directory it created. Bob issues the git commands on your behalf, so you do not need to work with Git yourself.

  1. Bob plans its approach and pauses for your approval before running any shell commands.

    The Tools awaiting approval section shows that Bob intends to execute a git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse command: a lightweight sparse clone that fetches the required subdirectory instead of the entire repository.

    Click Approve for task to authorize Bob to run this and all subsequent allowed commands for this task. This approval step is a built-in safety control: Bob executes terminal commands only after you consent.

  1. Bob is now executing the task. The Agentic Sidebar shows the sequence of tool calls it is making: it ran the sparse git clone command, then listed the files inside the _temp_repo temporary directory it created to verify the clone succeeded.

    • You can see _temp_repo has appeared in the Explorer panel on the left
    • The status at the bottom of the panel reads Working on it...

  1. Bob continues working autonomously. It has now drilled further into the cloned repository: the tool log shows it listing files in _temp_repo and then in _temp_repo\CBSA, navigating the directory tree to locate the src/base subdirectory. No action is required from you at this point; wait while Bob completes its work.

  1. Bob has located the target files. The tool-call log shows it navigated step by step through _temp_repo → CBSA → src → base, confirming the full path _temp_repo\CBSA\src\base. The status bar now reads Processing... as Bob copies the files from the temporary clone into your workspace. No action is needed; continue waiting.

  1. Bob pauses for a second approval. Having confirmed the file location, it now wants to run an xcopy command to copy the contents of _temp_repo\CBSA\src\base into a src\base folder in your workspace, then delete the temporary directory.

    Click Approve for task to authorize this final step. This copy-and-cleanup sequence is the behaviour you asked for in the original prompt.

    The documented run is on Windows.

    On macOS or Linux operating systems, Bob IDE proposes the equivalent cp command instead; approve it in the same way.

  1. Bob has completed the task. The Explorer panel now shows a src folder in the workspace, and the temporary _temp_repo directory has been removed as requested.

    Bob's completion summary in the panel confirms the Retrieved Structure: src/base/bms_src/ (9 BMS map definition files), src/base/cobol_copy/ (34 COBOL copybooks), src/base/cobol_src/ (32 COBOL source files) and src/base/README.md. All the CBSA application source files needed for the lab are now in place.

    TWO VALID FOLDER LAYOUTS

    Depending on how Bob copies the files, you may find the folder structure is either src/base/... directly in your workspace, or CBSA/src/base/... with a CBSA parent folder. Both are correct, and the lab steps work the same way in either case. The screenshot here shows src directly at the workspace root with no CBSA parent.

  1. In the Explorer panel, click the src folder to expand it and verify the lab files are present.

    If your structure has a CBSA parent folder:

    • Expand CBSA first
    • Then expand src inside it

    The Agentic Sidebar on the right confirms what you should find: src/base/bms_src/, src/base/cobol_copy/, src/base/cobol_src/ and src/base/README.md.

  1. Expanding src\base confirms the three core folders required for this lab are present:

    • bms_src — BMS map definitions, the screen layout files for the CBSA CICS application
    • cobol_copy — COBOL copybooks, the shared data structure definitions
    • cobol_src — the COBOL source programs

    You will also see README.md. These three folders contain all the mainframe application code you will work with throughout the lab.

  1. Expand bms_src to confirm it contains the 9 BMS map definition files (for example, BNK1ACC.bms and BNK1CAM.bms).

    Expand cobol_copy and cobol_src as well to confirm those folders are also populated before proceeding.

  1. In the bottom-right corner of the Agentic Sidebar, click New task. This clears the current conversation and opens a fresh task context, ensuring Bob starts the next instruction without any carry-over from the file-retrieval task you have completed.

docs.title: ix. Create the workspace rules
docs.text:
Rules are the always-on constraints: short, persistent instructions that Bob reads at the start of every task. Here they tell Bob where its documents, tools and diagrams belong— and how to name them —for the remainder of the lab.

  1. Continue in Agent mode. Paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar and hit Enter to execute:

    Create the following Bob rules (file in .bob/rules): 
- Documents must be stored in the docs/ directory. Documents specific to a program should be stored in a sub-directory of docs/ using the program name. For example, documents about BNKMENU should be stored in docs/BNKMENU/ directory.
- Tools must be stored in the tools/ directory.
- Schemas, drawings and graphs must be stored in graph/ directory.

Document, schemas, drawings and graphs file names must follow these conventions:

-- Prefix: program name (e.g., BNKMENU) if the document concerns a specific program, or CBSA for the application, or GLOBAL for cross-cutting documents

-- Document type: analysis, archi, docu, inv, plan, spec

-- Format: [PREFIX]-[TYPE]-[description].md

    Because the prompt spans multiple lines, Bob displays it as a collapsed pill in the input area rather than showing it inline. Click the pill to expand and review the full prompt text before it is sent.

  1. The expanded prompt preview dialog (Pasted text #1 - xx lines) shows the full instructions you are giving Bob: create a rules file at .bob/rules/ that defines the file-organisation conventions for this workspace.

    • Documents go in docs/, with per-program subdirectories
    • Tools go in tools/
    • Schemas, drawings and graphs go in graph/
    • All file names follow the [PREFIX]-[TYPE]-[description].md format

    Review the text to confirm it matches, then click Save to confirm the prompt and return it to the input field ready to send.

  1. Click the Send message button in the bottom-right corner (or hit Enter for an equivalent keyboard shortcut) to submit the file-organisation rules prompt to Bob.

  1. Bob begins executing the task immediately. It explores the workspace structure, then attempts to write .bob/rules/file-organisation.md. In the documented run the write failed, because the .bob/rules/ directory did not yet exist; the error Failed to write file .bob/rules/file-organisation.md is visible in the panel. Bob detects this automatically and requests permission to create the missing directory in the next step.

    Due to the non-deterministic nature of generative AI, you may not encounter the exact same issues. When issues are encountered, Bob often tries to debug them automatically.

  1. Bob has recognised that the write failed because .bob/rules/ does not exist, and requests permission to run mkdir .bob\rules — a shell command that creates the missing directory.

    Click Approve for task to allow Bob to create the directory and resume writing the rules file. The approval is required because the execute tool group (which controls shell command access) needs explicit user consent before running commands on your machine.

  1. After approving the mkdir command, a rules folder appears inside .bob in the Explorer panel. The Agentic Sidebar confirms the full recovery sequence: it detected the write failure, ran mkdir .bob\rules to create the directory, and is now actively writing the rules file. This .bob/rules/ directory is where Bob stores workspace-scoped rules — persistent instructions that Bob reads at the start of every task to guide its behaviour in this project.

  1. Bob has completed the task. In the Explorer panel, .bob/rules/file-organisation.md is now visible: a new rules file containing the file-organisation conventions you specified. The panel summarises what was written. Tools go in tools/ and schemas, drawings and graphs in graph/. All files follow the [PREFIX]-[TYPE]-[description].md naming convention:

    • Prefix: <PROGRAM>, CBSA or GLOBAL
    • Type: analysis / archi / docu / inv / plan / spec

    Bob will now apply these conventions automatically whenever it creates or places files in this workspace.

  1. With the file-organisation rules task complete and file-organisation.md confirmed in the Explorer, click New task in the lower-right corner of the Agentic Sidebar. This clears the current task context so that the next prompt starts fresh.

docs.title: x. Verify the environment
docs.text:
Before any module work begins, confirm that every piece of the environment is in place.

READINESS CHECK

Before proceeding, verify each of the following items:

  • Bob Settings → Add-ons lists IBM Bob Premium Package for Z
  • The Extensions view lists five installed extensions: the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z with its three companions (IBM Z Open Editor, Mermaid and Zowe Explorer) plus Draw.io Integration
  • The Agentic Sidebar's mode selector lists Z Code and Z Architect alongside Agent, Plan and Ask
  • The Bob PPZ L3 workspace is open and trusted (no Restricted Mode shield in the bottom-left corner)
  • The workspace contains src/base/ (or CBSA/src/base/) with bms_src, cobol_copy, cobol_src and README.md
  • The workspace contains .bob/rules/file-organisation.md

A WORD ON WORKING WITH GENERATIVE AI

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against.

Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool.

docs.title: xi. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Internal registration grants the general-purpose IBM Bob account tied to your w3id; the Premium Package for Z is a separate request through the w3 add-ons portal, approved manually within 24 to 48 hours and confirmed only by its appearance in Bob Settings → Add-ons. There is no approval email.
  • The IBM Bob Premium Package for Z installs from the Bob IDE's Extensions view and brings three companions with it: IBM Z Open Editor (language support), Mermaid (diagrams in the editor) and Zowe Explorer (z/OS datasets, USS files and jobs). The third-party Draw.io Integration extension completes the diagramming toolkit.
  • Two new modes — Z Code for implementing and explaining mainframe code and Z Architect for application analysis and architecture mapping — are the visible sign that the entitlement is live; if they are missing from the mode selector, the entitlement has not landed.
  • Bob in Agent mode retrieves the lab's source files for you with a sparse git clone, pausing at each Tools awaiting approval checkpoint; Approve for task is the control that lets it run the rest of a task without interruption.
  • The CBSA application arrives as src/base/ with 9 BMS maps, 34 copybooks and 32 COBOL programs; a CBSA/ parent folder is equally valid.
  • Workspace rules in .bob/rules/ govern where Bob files documents, tools and diagrams and how it names them. Bob reads them at the start of every task, which is why they are established before any module begins.
  • New task between prompts clears the context window so that each instruction starts clean.

Registration and setup are complete. The first hands-on module, Module 1 | Understanding the CICS Banking Sample Application, begins from this workspace.

docs.text: GETTING STARTED

docs.title: i. Before you begin
docs.text:
These instructions apply to IBM Business Partners. IBM regular employees have their own instructions available via IBMers | Registration and setup, which routes the Premium Package request through the w3 add-ons portal.

Before diving into the hands-on modules, complete the following registration and setup steps to prepare your machine with an authenticated IBM Bob account entitled to the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z (PPZ), along with a local copy of the CBSA sample banking application that the first two hands-on modules build upon. The work proceeds in six stages:

  • Request the Premium Package for Z entitlement through IBM Technology Zone, which provisions both the IBM Bob service and the package against your IBMid
  • Install and authenticate the Bob IDE on your local machine, then bind it to the entitlement
  • Install the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z extension and its companions from the Extensions view, plus the Draw.io Integration extension used for diagramming
  • Create a fresh project workspace
  • Retrieve the CBSA application source files (COBOL programs, copybooks and BMS screen maps) with Bob in Agent mode
  • Establish the workspace rules that govern where Bob files its documents, tools and diagrams throughout the lab

docs.title: ii. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure that you have each of the following in hand before starting; most setup stalls trace back to one of these.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN

  • Valid IBMid credentials (the same IBMid you use to sign in to IBM Technology Zone)
  • Administrative rights to install software on your local machine
  • Internet access to github.com — the lab files are retrieved from a public repository

No Intranet or VPN connection is required.

THIS LAB REQUIRES THE PREMIUM PACKAGE FOR Z

Without the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z (PPZ) entitlement, IBM Bob can still open and read mainframe code, though the Z Code and Z Architect modes and the specifically-trained capabilities that the package provides will be missing. If neither mode appears in your Agentic Sidebar by the end of this chapter, the entitlement has not been linked to your Bob account.

ALREADY HAVE IBM BOB?

An existing IBM Bob account (a Free Trial, for example) does not carry the Premium Package for Z. Complete the entitlement request in section iii regardless; if the Bob IDE is already installed on your machine, you can skip the download in section iv and go straight to signing in.

docs.title: iii. Request the Premium Package for Z entitlement
docs.text:
Business Partner reservation requests for IBM Bob Premium Packages are made separately from the requests for a general-purpose IBM Bob account. In other words: requesting an IBM Bob account (such as you completed earlier) does not carry entitlements for any Premium Packages (such as PPZ). A separate reservation request must be filed for such entitlements, which the following steps will guide you through.

  1. Requests for Premium Package for Z entitlements are made via IBM Technology Zone. Visit the following collection to begin the process:

    URL: https://techzone.ibm.com/collection/bob-business-partner-enablement/environments

    From the left-hand side of the page, click the Environments tab.

  1. Four options will be available:

    • Request entitlement for IBM Bob Enterprise
    • Request entitlement for IBM Bob Premium Package for i
    • Request entitlement for IBM Bob Premium Package for Z
    • Request entitlement for IBM Bob Premium Package for Java

    Click the Reserve it button below the Request entitlement for IBM Bob Premium Package for Z tile.

  1. Step 1: General of the configuration process will ask you to specify a Name and Description for your reservation. When ready, click Next in the bottom-right corner to continue.

  1. Step 2: Business purpose must be set to Test in order to bypass the need for an opportunity number. If you mistakenly click the wrong option, or if the reservation system does not allow you to continue without an opportunity number, exit out from this page and try again (making sure to only click Test). When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 3: Deployment will ask you to specify the Geography for your deployment. Select the data center location that is closest to you. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 4: Scheduling will ask you to specify the go-live and termination dates for your entitlement. Choose a window that comfortably covers the time you expect to spend on this lab. If the entitlement lapses before you finish, you can submit a new request using these same instructions. When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 5: Configure can be left blank (default state of "There is nothing to configure here.") When ready, click Next to continue.

  1. Step 6: Review and submit will ask you to review your configuration settings before submitting the request. Scroll down through your reservation details and, if you approve, check the I agree to IBM Technology Zone's terms & conditions and user security policies. box at the bottom of the page. When ready, click Submit to initiate the reservation request.

  1. The web browser will redirect automatically to IBM Technology Zone's My requests dashboard. From this page, you can monitor and track the progression of your reservation request as it moves from Scheduled to Provisioning to Ready.

    Average deployment times are roughly 5 minutes or less.

    Wait until the request is marked as Ready before advancing.

  1. When the reservation is Ready, you will receive an email to your inbox providing you with a link to the environment and the same details will also be accessible via the My requests dashboard (where you were tracking the reservation request).

    Click either the View your request link in the email body OR click the arrow to the left of your reservation name on the My requests dashboard to expand details about the request.

  1. Both links will direct to the IBM Bob dashboard:

    URL: https://bob.ibm.com/admin

    Authenticate and log in using your IBMid — the same one you used to sign in to IBM Technology Zone. The entitlement you just requested is associated with it.

  1. The web browser will redirect to a welcome splash screen reading "Welcome [your username]!" where you are prompted to Choose workspace.

    If you previously registered for IBM Bob by another route (such as a Free Trial), the default option below this may display text such as Free Trial or something else entirely.

    • Click the box below Choose workspace to open a drop-down menu
    • Your request via IBM Technology Zone will have added a new option to this list, similar to TECHZONE-BobathonV2 (us-east): this is your newly-provisioned Premium Package for Z entitlement
    • Select the TECHZONE-... option as your workspace and then continue with the login

    EXACT WORDING VARIES BY REGION

    The label of the workspace depends on the geography you selected in Step 5 and may not read exactly as it does in the screen capture. Look for the option prefixed with TECHZONE.

  1. The web browser will automatically load into the IBM Bob dashboard.

    • Verify in the top-left corner that the TECHZONE-... workspace is selected for Organization
    • Click the Subscription tab to view your plan type and seat count, as well as your Bobcoin balance
    • Towards the bottom of the panel, under the Premium packages section, an IBM Z tile marked as Active confirms that your IBM Bob account is now linked to (and entitled for use with) the Premium Package for Z license

docs.title: iv. Install and authenticate the Bob IDE
docs.text:
With the entitlement provisioned, install the Bob IDE (if you have not already done so) and sign in with the same IBMid.

  1. If the Bob IDE is not yet installed on your machine, download and install it now. Select the version that matches your operating system.

  1. Open the Bob IDE and press Log in to Bob.

  1. Press Allow on the pop-up window, followed by Open on the subsequent pop-up window.

  1. On the IBM Verify sign-in page, expand the "Choose an option" drop-down and press IBMid. Sign in with the same IBMid that you used on IBM Technology Zone.

docs.title: v. Install the Premium Package for Z extension
docs.text:
With the entitlement in place, the next stage installs the extension that delivers it inside the Bob IDE. The Premium Package arrives through the Bob IDE's own Extensions view and brings three companion extensions with it.

  1. Click the Extensions icon in the left Activity Bar (the square icon), or press Ctrl+Shift+X. This opens the Extensions Marketplace panel where you can search for and install the extensions required for this lab.

  1. The Extensions panel opens in the left sidebar, with the Search Extensions in Marketplace search bar at the top.

  1. In the search bar, filter on the following text:

    Premium Package For Z

    The top result should be IBM Bob Premium Package for Z with IBM marked as the publisher. Several similar-named extensions appear below it — make sure you select the correct one.

  1. Click the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z result to open its detail page. Verify that the publisher is IBM and that the version is 3.0.0 or higher, which this lab requires. The detail page confirms this is the correct extension before you commit to installing it.

  1. Click the Install button on the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z detail page.

  1. Click the Clear Extensions Search Results icon (next to the search box). Clearing the search filter resets the Extensions view so you can see your installed extensions and verify that the package components were properly added.

  1. Under the INSTALLED section of the Extensions sidebar, verify that four extensions have been installed as part of the package:

    EXTENSION PUBLISHER PURPOSE IBM Bob Premium Package for Z IBM Mainframe-specific AI agents, modes and workflows IBM Z Open Editor IBM Language support and syntax highlighting for COBOL, PL/I, HLASM, REXX and JCL Mermaid MermaidChart Renders architecture and flow diagrams directly within the editor Zowe Explorer Zowe Interaction with z/OS datasets, Unix System Services (USS) files and jobs

docs.title: vi. Bind the IDE to your entitlement
docs.text:
The extension is installed, but the Bob IDE still needs to be pointed at the TechZone workspace that carries your entitlement. Two settings complete the connection.

  1. Look towards the bottom-right corner of the Bob IDE interface. Along the bottom edge of the interface there will be an interactable button labelled Bob Settings — click this button to open the Settings panel.

  1. From the Settings panel, make sure the General tab (left side) is the one being displayed.

    • Locate the Team setting, which by default at this stage might be set to Trial or some other variation

  1. Further down the panel, adjacent to the Add ons setting, you should now see IBM Bob Premium Package for Z displayed.

  1. Bob continues working autonomously. It has now drilled further into the cloned repository: the tool log shows it listing files in _temp_repo and then in _temp_repo\CBSA, navigating the directory tree to locate the src/base subdirectory. No action is required from you at this point; wait while Bob completes its work.

  1. Bob has located the target files. The tool-call log shows it navigated step by step through _temp_repo → CBSA → src → base, confirming the full path _temp_repo\CBSA\src\base. The status bar now reads Processing... as Bob copies the files from the temporary clone into your workspace. No action is needed; continue waiting.

  1. Bob pauses for a second approval. Having confirmed the file location, it now wants to run an xcopy command to copy the contents of _temp_repo\CBSA\src\base into a src\base folder in your workspace, then delete the temporary directory.

    Click Approve for task to authorize this final step. This copy-and-cleanup sequence is the behaviour you asked for in the original prompt.

    The documented run is on Windows operating systems.

    On macOS or Linux, Bob proposes the equivalent cp command instead. Approve it in the same way.

  1. Bob has completed the task. The Explorer panel now shows a src folder in the workspace, and the temporary _temp_repo directory has been removed as requested. Bob's completion summary in the panel confirms the Retrieved Structure: src/base/bms_src/ (9 BMS map definition files), src/base/cobol_copy/ (34 COBOL copybooks), src/base/cobol_src/ (32 COBOL source files) and src/base/README.md. All the CBSA application source files needed for the lab are now in place.

    TWO VALID FOLDER LAYOUTS

    Depending on how Bob copies the files, you may find the folder structure is either src/base/... directly in your workspace, or CBSA/src/base/... with a CBSA parent folder. Both are correct, and the lab steps work the same way in either case. The screenshot here shows src directly at the workspace root with no CBSA parent.

  1. In the Explorer panel, click the src folder to expand it and verify the lab files are present.

    If your structure has a CBSA parent folder:

    • Expand CBSA first
    • Then expand src inside it

    The Agentic Sidebar on the right confirms what you should find: src/base/bms_src/, src/base/cobol_copy/, src/base/cobol_src/ and src/base/README.md.

  1. Expanding src\base confirms the three core folders required for this lab are present:

    • bms_src — BMS map definitions, the screen layout files for the CBSA CICS application
    • cobol_copy — COBOL copybooks, the shared data structure definitions
    • cobol_src — the COBOL source programs

    You will also see README.md. These three folders contain all the mainframe application code you will work with throughout the lab.

  1. Expand bms_src to confirm it contains the 9 BMS map definition files (for example, BNK1ACC.bms and BNK1CAM.bms).

    Expand cobol_copy and cobol_src as well to confirm those folders are also populated before proceeding.

  1. In the bottom-right corner of the Agentic Sidebar, click New task. This clears the current conversation and opens a fresh task context, ensuring Bob starts the next instruction without any carry-over from the file-retrieval task you have completed.

docs.title: x. Create the workspace rules
docs.text:
Rules are the always-on constraints you first met in Module 3 | Tailor of the Climbing the AI Maturity Curve courseware: short, persistent instructions that Bob reads at the start of every task. Here they tell Bob where its documents, tools and diagrams belong — and how to name them — for the rest of the lab.

  1. Continue in Agent mode. Paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar and hit Enter to execute:

    Create the following Bob rules (file in .bob/rules): 
- Documents must be stored in the docs/ directory. Documents specific to a program should be stored in a sub-directory of docs/ using the program name. For example, documents about BNKMENU should be stored in docs/BNKMENU/ directory.
- Tools must be stored in the tools/ directory.
- Schemas, drawings and graphs must be stored in graph/ directory.

Document, schemas, drawings and graphs file names must follow these conventions:

-- Prefix: program name (e.g., BNKMENU) if the document concerns a specific program, or CBSA for the application, or GLOBAL for cross-cutting documents

-- Document type: analysis, archi, docu, inv, plan, spec

-- Format: [PREFIX]-[TYPE]-[description].md

    Because the prompt spans multiple lines, Bob displays it as a collapsed pill in the input area rather than showing it inline. Click the pill to expand and review the full prompt text before it is sent.

  1. The expanded prompt preview dialog (Pasted text #1 - xx lines) shows the full instructions you are giving Bob: create a rules file at .bob/rules/ that defines the file-organisation conventions for this workspace.

    • Documents go in docs/, with per-program subdirectories
    • Tools go in tools/
    • Schemas, drawings and graphs go in graph/
    • All file names follow the [PREFIX]-[TYPE]-[description].md format

    Review the text to confirm it matches, then click Save to confirm the prompt and return it to the input field ready to send.

  1. Click the Send message button in the bottom-right corner (or hit Enter for an equivalent keyboard shortcut) to submit the file-organisation rules prompt to Bob.

  1. Bob begins executing the task immediately. It explores the workspace structure, then attempts to write .bob/rules/file-organisation.md. In the documented run the write failed, because the .bob/rules/ directory did not yet exist; the error Failed to write file .bob/rules/file-organisation.md is visible in the panel. Bob detects this automatically and requests permission to create the missing directory in the next step.

    Due to the non-deterministic nature of generative AI, you may not encounter the exact same issues. When issues are encountered, Bob often tries to debug them automatically.

  1. Bob has recognised that the write failed because .bob/rules/ does not exist, and requests permission to run mkdir .bob\rules — a shell command that creates the missing directory.

    Click Approve for task to allow Bob to create the directory and resume writing the rules file. The approval is required because the execute tool group (which controls shell command access) needs explicit user consent before running commands on your machine.

  1. After approving the mkdir command, a rules folder appears inside .bob in the Explorer panel. The Agentic Sidebar confirms the full recovery sequence: it detected the write failure, ran mkdir .bob\rules to create the directory, and is now actively writing the rules file. This .bob/rules/ directory is where Bob stores workspace-scoped rules — persistent instructions that Bob reads at the start of every task to guide its behaviour in this project.

  1. Bob has completed the task. In the Explorer panel, .bob/rules/file-organisation.md is now visible: a new rules file containing the file-organisation conventions you specified. The panel summarises what was written. Tools go in tools/ and schemas, drawings and graphs in graph/. All files follow the [PREFIX]-[TYPE]-[description].md naming convention:

    • Prefix: <PROGRAM>, CBSA or GLOBAL
    • Type: analysis / archi / docu / inv / plan / spec

    Bob will now apply these conventions automatically whenever it creates or places files in this workspace.

  1. With the file-organisation rules task complete and file-organisation.md confirmed in the Explorer, click New task in the lower-right corner of the Agentic Sidebar. This clears the current task context so that the next prompt starts fresh.

docs.title: xi. Verify the environment
docs.text:
Before any module work begins, confirm that every piece of the environment is in place.

READINESS CHECK

Before proceeding, verify each of the following items:

  • Bob Settings → General shows the TECHZONE-... workspace as your Team, and the Install addon operation for the Premium Package for Z has completed
  • The Extensions view lists five installed extensions: the IBM Bob Premium Package for Z with its three companions (IBM Z Open Editor, Mermaid and Zowe Explorer) plus Draw.io Integration
  • The Agentic Sidebar's mode selector lists Z Code and Z Architect alongside Agent, Plan and Ask
  • The Bob PPZ L3 workspace is open and trusted (no Restricted Mode shield in the bottom-left corner)
  • The workspace contains src/base/ (or CBSA/src/base/) with bms_src, cobol_copy, cobol_src and README.md
  • The workspace contains .bob/rules/file-organisation.md

A WORD ON WORKING WITH GENERATIVE AI

IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against.

Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool.
