docs.text: MODULE 1 | ANALYZE

docs.title: UNDERSTANDING THE CICS BANKING SAMPLE APPLICATION
i. Understanding the codebase
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Analyze module for the hands-on enablement. [3 min]

Before any modernization or maintenance effort can begin, engineers must first understand how a legacy application behaves. Much like Literate Coding allows developers to express change through natural language, Agentic AI enables developers to explore and understand unfamiliar codebases using conversational prompts.

Tracing programs, copybooks, BMS maps and data stores by hand means reading across thousands of lines of COBOL. IBM Bob can analyze the same codebase in minutes and produce program documentation, architecture diagrams and change impact assessments from it.

The effect is similar to working alongside a senior mainframe engineer: someone who can explain decades of accumulated business logic and say what breaks before you change it.

In this module you will work with the CICS Banking Sample Application (CBSA), an enterprise-grade z/OS reference application. It simulates core retail banking operations: customer onboarding and account management, together with deposits, withdrawals and fund transfers.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
A deep understanding of the existing application reduces migration risk and improves modernization outcomes.

Legacy-system analysis is particularly valuable when working with:

  • Large COBOL applications containing decades of business logic
  • Poorly documented systems where original developers are unavailable
  • Shared copybooks and BMS (Basic Mapping Support) maps where a single field change can ripple across many artifacts
  • Interdependent programs spread across presentation, business logic and data tiers
  • Modernization initiatives targeting Java, Python or cloud-native platforms
TASK WITH: Manual Analysis WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for Z Program documentation 1–2 days of analysis and writing Minutes of generation Architecture diagrams 2–3 days of manual creation Minutes of automatic generation Impact analysis Manual cross-referencing of every copybook and program Automatic, traceable blast-radius report Updates Difficult to maintain Instant regeneration

docs.title: iii. Explaining a program with Bob Workflows
docs.text:
Begin with the built-in Explain code workflow to generate business-focused documentation for BANKDATA, the batch program that initializes CBSA's application data.

  1. Click the Explorer tab along the left edge of the Bob IDE.

    • The Bob PPZ L3 workspace from the Registration and setup chapter should already be open inside the Explorer tab.
    • Its src/base/ folder (or CBSA/src/base/) holds bms_src, cobol_copy, and cobol_src.
    CAN'T LOCATE THE DIRECTORY?

    If this is not the case:

    • Click Open Folder to expose the File Explorer view
    • Drill down into the Bob PPZ L3 folder and click Open

    ABOUT THE SCREENSHOTS IN THIS MODULE

    The screenshots were captured in a workspace folder named ppz-demo, with the three source folders sitting at its root. Your workspace is named Bob PPZ L3 and holds the same three folders under src/base/. The steps are otherwise identical.

  1. Near the top-right of the IBM Bob sidebar, click the Bob workflows button (the play icon) to open the workflow catalog. If a workspace picker appears first, select Run Workflow in Bob PPZ L3.

    WHAT ARE BOB WORKFLOWS?

    Workflows guide you through complex tasks step by step using built-in AI prompts. Instead of writing a prompt from scratch, you answer a few guided questions and Bob runs a multi-step analysis on your behalf.

  1. From the list of available workflows, locate Explain code and click Start.

  1. The Explain code workflow produces an explanation of the selected program. It analyzes the code with its copybook references and identifies the program logic, business rules and data usage.

    Under Program selection, click Browse files.

  1. In the file picker, navigate to src › base › cobol_src and select BANKDATA.cbl.

    Click Select File.

  1. Confirm that BANKDATA.cbl appears as the selected file, then click Continue with selection.

  1. Bob will ask which perspective the explanation should be written for.

    Select Business and click Confirm.

    EXPLANATION PERSPECTIVES

    The workflow offers three perspectives: Architect, Developer and Business. Each perspective produces a separate file with content tailored to that job role. You may re-run the workflow later to compare all three.

  1. Bob extracts the program's variables and generates the explanation.

    • When the workflow finishes, the Workflow results section shows where the explanation was saved.
    • Click the docs/explain/business_BANKDATA.md link to open it.

  1. Review the generated Business Summary & Analysis.

    Bob describes BANKDATA in business terms:

    • Its primary function: a batch data generation utility
    • The runtime parameters it accepts: START-KEY, END-KEY, STEP-KEY and RANDOM-SEED
    • The business rules it enforces, such as credit score assignment, account portfolio creation across product types and control record tracking for downstream reconciliation

    TRY IT WITH A PROMPT INSTEAD

    You can achieve a similar result without the workflow by typing /explain @src/base/cobol_src/BANKDATA.cbl in the chat. Bob will adapt the explanation to the currently active mode. With this approach Bob may not save the explanation automatically, so you may need to follow up with a prompt such as save the BANKDATA explanation.

docs.title: iv. Documenting the CBSA architecture with Z Architect mode
docs.text:
The program explanation covers a single program in depth. Next you will have Bob document the architecture of the entire application: its programs, databases and major dependencies.

  1. Near the bottom of the Agentic Sidebar, press the Mode toggle to expand the list of modes and select Z Architect.

    SWITCHING BETWEEN DIFFERENT AGENTIC MODES

    The label assigned to the Mode toggle button will change to reflect the name of the mode that the Agentic Sidebar currently has active. For example, if in the Agent mode, the toggle button will read as Agent. For the sake of clarity, when instructing you to change the Agentic Mode type, this documentation will refer to this toggle button as the Mode toggle.

  1. With Z Architect mode active, copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar session window:

    Visually document the CBSA architecture in a .md file representing programs, databases, and major dependencies.

    With the prompt entered, hit Enter or press the Send button to the right of the chat interface.

    WHY Z ARCHITECT MODE?

    Z Architect mode specializes in creating architecture diagrams and analyzing application flows, which suits it to mapping inter-program relationships and producing structured documentation.

  1. Bob drafts a to-do list for the task: exploring the workspace, analyzing program dependencies and database access, and generating the documentation.

    Click Approve todo tools for task so Bob can update its progress without asking again.

    APPROVING TOOL REQUESTS

    Depending on your permission settings, Bob may also ask you to approve individual file reads or other tool calls as it works. Click Approve for each request as it appears.

  1. When all tasks are completed, Bob summarizes the highlights covered in the documentation, including:

    • System tiers: 29 COBOL programs split across presentation drivers, business logic services, an asynchronous credit bureau simulation and utilities
    • Persistence architecture: VSAM KSDS files (CUSTOMER and ABNDFILE) and Db2 tables (ACCOUNT, PROCTRAN and CONTROL)
    • End-to-end sequence flows such as customer onboarding, account creation and funds transfer
    • A copybook dependency matrix mapping the shared copybooks to the programs that use them

    Click the docs/cbsa_architecture.md link at the bottom of the response to open the full document.

    THE FILE NAME MAY DIFFER

    The workspace rules you created during setup tell Bob where to file its documents and how to name them. Bob may therefore save this document under a name that follows the [PREFIX]-[TYPE]-[description].md convention rather than the name shown in the screenshot. Follow the link in Bob's response.

  1. The Executive Summary & System Overview describes CBSA as a CICS application built on IBM CICS Transaction Server for z/OS, Db2 for z/OS and VSAM. It notes the clear separation between the presentation, business service and data layers.

    Scroll down to the High-Level Layered Architecture diagram to see how BNKMENU routes users to each screen driver.

  1. Continue scrolling to the Detailed Program Architecture & Catalog. Bob lists four things for every program: its transaction ID, its BMS mapset, its source file and the business services it calls. The result is a complete and navigable inventory of the application.

    OPTIONAL: GO FURTHER WITH ARCHITECTURE PROMPTS

    If you have token budget to spare, try these variations in Z Architect mode and compare the results:

    • Build an architecture diagram (in draw.io) illustrating the program dependencies of the CBSA application.
    • Create documentation with comprehensive call graphs of all programs in the workspace, organized by functional topics.

    Draw.io output produces an editable diagram that you can refine with follow-up prompts. One example is asking Bob to color-code the SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE access on each table.

docs.title: v. Analyzing the impact of a field change
docs.text:
A common maintenance question on the mainframe sounds simple: "What happens if I change this field?" A single copybook field can be shared by BMS maps, programs and runtime resources. In this section, Bob traces the full blast radius of shrinking one field before any code is touched.

  1. In the Explorer tab, expand the cobol_copy folder and open BANKMAP.cpy.

    Locate Line 14, which defines the company name input field:

    02  COMPANYI  PIC X(40).

  1. Highlight the entire line, then right-click and select IBM Bob › Add to Context to add the field to your active chat session.

  1. In the chat window, confirm the field has been added as context. It will appear as a tag reading BANKMAP.cpy:14.

    Before sending any instructions, press the Mode toggle and make sure Z Architect is selected.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar chat, type or paste the following prompt:

    What would be the impact of changing this field to 10? Generate Impact-Analysis.md

    Then hit Enter or press the Send button to execute the instruction.

  1. Bob recognizes the request and loads its impact-analysis skill. It then drafts a to-do list: read the copybook, identify every program that uses it, perform the dependency analysis and ask clarifying questions. Click Approve todo tools for task.

    APPROVING TOOL REQUESTS

    You may be asked to approve roughly 4–5 additional tool requests in sequence: skill requests, individual file reads and query requests. Click Approve for each one as it appears. Each approval allows Bob to complete the next step in tracing which artifacts reference COMPANYI.

  1. Before writing the report, Bob asks clarifying questions. For example, it may notice that the BMS source defines the field with a different length than the copybook, or that BANKMAP.cpy is referenced under a different member name.

    When prompted, select the option stating that the change is hypothetical/for analysis purposes and that Bob should document the full blast radius: the BMS source, the COBOL copybook and all downstream effects.

    RESPONSES MAY VARY

    Bob's questions are generated from its analysis, so the exact wording and number of questions may differ from the screenshot. Choose the option closest to a hypothetical, full blast-radius analysis. If Bob asks whether to include a Z Understand analysis, select the option to continue with the local analysis results only. Skip this step if you are not asked.

  1. When all tasks are completed, Bob saves the report to a date-stamped folder under bobz/impact-analysis/ and summarizes its Key Findings in the chat:

    • What must change: four artifacts

      • Both the input (COMPANYI) and output (COMPANYO) fields in BANKMAP.cpy
      • The DFHMDF LENGTH in bms_src/BNK1MAI.bms
      • The physical BMS map load module, reassembled and refreshed with CICS NEWCOPY
      • BNKMENU.cbl, recompiled and relinked

    • Most critical risk: if the copybook changes but the BMS source is not reassembled, the physical and symbolic maps fall out of sync by 30 bytes. Every subsequent field would be read or written at the wrong offset, causing silent data corruption or an ASRA abend

    • Inevitable business impact: the company name literal displayed on the main menu would be silently truncated, making the application title unrecognizable to users

    Click the report link in the response to open IMPACT-ANALYSIS.md.

  1. Review the Change Summary. Bob restates the change specification and explains why it cannot be made in isolation. It then captures the system context: the technologies involved, the entry point (BNKMENU.cbl under transaction OMEN) and the known dependencies.

  1. Scroll to the Scope Definition. Bob separates what is in scope from what is out of scope, and explains why.

    Notice that BNK1DDM.cpy also contains a field named COMPANYI, yet Bob correctly excludes it because it belongs to a different mapset. This is the kind of false positive that a plain text search would get wrong.

  1. Continue to the System Overview. The Components Analyzed table lists every affected artifact with its type, the change required and an impact level. It gives teams a ready-made checklist for planning the change.

    DIAGRAM NOT RENDERING?

    If the System Context Diagram shows a parse error instead of a diagram, Bob generated Mermaid syntax that the previewer could not read (often caused by special characters such as parentheses in node labels). Ask Bob to fix it with a follow-up prompt such as Fix the Mermaid syntax error in the System Context Diagram of IMPACT-ANALYSIS.md.

docs.title: vi. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Bob Workflows turn complex analysis tasks into guided, repeatable steps
  • Explanations can be tailored to Architect, Developer or Business audiences
  • Z Architect mode can document an entire application's programs, data stores and dependencies in minutes
  • Impact analysis traces the full blast radius of a change across copybooks, BMS maps, programs and runtime resources
  • Bob distinguishes true dependencies from look-alike fields, reducing false positives
  • Understanding change impact before touching code reduces risk and prevents production incidents

The next module shifts from analysis to change. Building on what you learned here, you will have Bob plan a new feature for CBSA and then write the COBOL that delivers it. Continue to Module 2 | Implementing a new feature in COBOL.

docs.title: Implementing a new feature in COBOL
docs.text: MODULE 2 | BUILD

docs.title: IMPLEMENTING A NEW FEATURE IN COBOL
i. From understanding to building
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Build module for the hands-on enablement. [3 min]

In the previous module you used IBM Bob to understand the CICS Banking Sample Application: what each program does, how the application is layered, and what a single field change would cost you.

This module puts that understanding to work. You will ask Bob to plan a new feature, review that plan as a human, and then have Bob write the COBOL to deliver it. Today, a bank teller connected to our hypothetical CICS application can only look up a customer by their numeric customer number. In the steps ahead, you will add the ability to search for a customer by email address.

The pattern matters more than the feature itself. Plan feature changes first before you ultimately implement and build them. A plan is quick to read and costs little to change or throw away. Generated code that nobody planned costs far more to review and to undo.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
Adding a feature to a mainframe application is rarely a single-file edit. A new lookup path can touch the BMS screen and the screen driver, a new business service, and the COMMAREA contract between them, and the VSAM record layout itself.

Agentic AI is valuable here because it:

  • Grounds the plan in the real codebase rather than in assumptions about how the application "probably" works
  • Surfaces gaps early, such as a field that the documentation claims exists but the copybook does not declare
  • Follows existing conventions by reusing the patterns already present in neighboring programs
  • Keeps a human in the loop, since every file change is proposed, reviewed and approved before it is implemented
TASK WITH: Manual Analysis WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for Z Design analysis Days of tracing programs and copybooks Minutes, grounded in the actual source Plan documentation Often skipped or written after the fact Produced first, as a reviewable artifact Code generation Hand-written, convention drift likely Follows the patterns in the existing suite Syntax verification Compile, read the errors and repeat Diagnostics plus a manual cross-check on request

docs.title: iii. Planning the change with Z Code mode
docs.text:
1. Near the bottom of the Agentic Sidebar, press the Mode toggle to expand the list of modes and select Z Code.

    WHY Z CODE MODE?

    Z Code mode specializes in detailed analysis, documentation and generation of COBOL programs. Z Architect mode reasons about how the application fits together. Z Code mode works at the level of program structure: paragraphs, copybooks and CICS commands.

  1. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar session window:

    What is the plan to implement customer search by email? Create CBSA-plan-email-search.md

    With the prompt entered, hit Enter or press the Send button to the right of the chat interface.

    ASK FOR A PLAN FIRST

    This prompt asks for a plan only. It does not ask Bob to write the feature. Asking for a plan first gives you a document you can review, correct and share with your team before a single line of COBOL is generated.

  1. Bob drafts a to-do list covering the workspace exploration, the dependency analysis and the creation of the plan file. Click Approve todo tools for task.

    APPROVING TOOL REQUESTS

    If auto-approval is turned off, Bob will also ask permission for individual file reads and queries as it works. Click Approve for each request as it appears.

  1. When the task completes, Bob summarizes its key findings from the codebase and the structure of the plan it produced. Read this summary carefully before opening the file.

    Bob makes two key observations:

    • A critical gap: the architecture ER diagram describes an email field on the customer record, but CUSTOMER.cpy does not declare it. No email variable exists anywhere in the codebase, so adding that field is the prerequisite for everything else.
    • A VSAM constraint: the CUSTOMER file is a KSDS keyed only on sort code and customer number. With no alternate index on email, the search must be a full sequential browse using the same STARTBR / READNEXT / ENDBR pattern already used elsewhere in the suite.

    Bob also makes an explicit design decision: create a new service rather than extend the existing INQCUST program, so that the five existing callers of INQCUST are not broken.

    THIS IS THE REVIEW STEP

    A plan that contradicts what you know about your system is useful: the disagreement surfaced before any code was written. Read the design decision, the scope and the risks sections. If you disagree, say so in a follow-up prompt before any code is generated.

docs.title: iv. Implementing the plan
docs.text:
1. Open CBSA-plan-email-search.md from the Explorer tab and review the full document. It holds the executive summary, a current-state analysis with a diagram of how customer lookup works today, the key programs table and the email field gap.

    THE FILE LOCATION MAY DIFFER

    The workspace rules you created during setup send Bob's documents to the docs/ folder. Bob may therefore have filed the plan there instead of at the workspace root. Follow the link in Bob's response.

    With the plan reviewed, send a follow-up prompt asking Bob to begin implementing it. For example:

    According to the implementation plan, update the CUSTOMER data structures
    • After copy and pasting the instruction above, hit Enter to execute the request.
    • Bob requests permission to use its COBOL code-generation skill.
    • Click Approve once to authorize it for this step, or Approve skill tools for task to authorize it for the remainder of the task.
    OPTIONAL: REFERENCING THE PLAN FILE DIRECTLY

    You can point Bob at the plan explicitly using the @ symbol in the chat bar, which inserts the correct path without you having to copy it manually:

    Use the @CBSA-plan-email-search.md file to implement the change

    Alternatively, right-click the file in the Explorer panel and select Copy Path, then paste the path into your prompt.

  1. Work through the plan step by step, approving each request as it appears. If auto-approve is turned off, Bob will prompt you before each individual change.

    As Bob applies the changes, the editor shows each modification as a diff: green lines indicate additions or new content, and red lines indicate removals or replaced content. The chat footer tracks how many files have changed, with Show all and Undo all controls available at any time.

  1. When the implementation completes, Bob summarizes the program it built. In this example it created cobol_src/INQEMAIL.cbl, named after the existing INQCUST convention and using the newly created SRCHEML.cpy copybook as its COMMAREA contract.

    The section structure table shows that Bob followed the conventions of the surrounding suite rather than inventing its own:

    • An entry-point section that validates the email is not blank
    • A browse section implementing the STARTBR / READNEXT loop with retry handling
    • A close-browse section called from every exit path
    • A populate-COMMAREA section
    • A CICS abend-handling section

docs.title: v. Verifying the generated code
docs.text:
Generated code is a starting point. Bob can check its own work. In addition to your own review and checks, consider making a habit of asking Bob to review its own work, too, before treating the code as a deliverable.

  1. Within the Agentic Sidebar chat, copy and paste the following prompt:

    Verify the syntax of the INQEMAIL.cbl program

    Hit Enter or press the Send button to execute the instruction.

  1. Bob runs its diagnostic tooling and reports the results, then performs a manual cross-check of the artifacts it created.

    Three details in this output deserve attention:

    • The remaining warning is explained. Bob flags an unused-variable warning on the abend-handling section and assesses it as an expected false positive. That section is the target of a CICS HANDLE ABEND, so the CICS runtime activates it instead of a COBOL PERFORM. The same pattern appears in every program in the suite.
    • The cross-check is field by field. Bob confirms every field in the new COMMAREA copybook and in the updated customer record layout is correctly referenced, and verifies its CICS API usage against the existing INQCUST.cbl as a reference implementation.
    • A real defect was found and fixed. During the review Bob identified a string-continuation operator that is not valid IBM Enterprise COBOL syntax and corrected it.

    CLEAN DIAGNOSTICS ARE ONLY THE FIRST CHECK

    Clean diagnostics mean the program is syntactically sound and internally consistent. They do not guarantee that the feature behaves correctly. This requires further validation from a human-in-the-loop (you).

    The plan's testing section lists functional test cases, including edge cases, that still need to be executed against a running region before this change could be considered complete.

docs.title: vi. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Asking for a plan before asking for code produces a reviewable artifact and a better result
  • Bob grounds its plan in the real codebase, surfacing gaps that documentation alone would hide
  • Design decisions are made explicit, such as creating a new service rather than breaking existing callers
  • Generated COBOL follows the conventions already present in the surrounding programs
  • Every file change is proposed as a reviewable diff and requires your approval before it is committed
  • Asking Bob to verify its own work catches real defects and explains the warnings it chooses to leave in place
  • Syntax verification is a checkpoint on the way to functional testing, which is still required

The next module moves from one program to a whole chain of them. Working on a second CICS application, GenApp, you will have Bob find the validation rules that are duplicated across its policy programs and consolidate them into a single shared service. Continue to Module 3 | Monolithic COBOL refactoring and service integration.

docs.title: Monolithic COBOL refactoring and service integration
docs.text: MODULE 3 | REFACTOR

docs.title: MONOLITHIC COBOL REFACTORING AND SERVICE INTEGRATION
i. From duplication to a shared service
docs.text:
Christopher Bienko (AI Enablement GTM Product Manager) provides an overview of the Refactor module for the hands-on enablement. [4 min]

Each of the GenApp policy programs validates incoming requests in its own code. The same checks are written out separately in the programs that add, update and delete a policy — so a change to one rule has to be made in several places.

In this module you will use IBM Bob to consolidate that logic. Bob will identify the validation rules and map everything that depends on them, move them into a single service program called LGPOLVAL, and update the original programs to call that service in place of their own checks.

The programs you will work with across Module 3 | Refactor include:

PROGRAM WHAT IT DOES LGAPDB01 Adds a policy LGUPDB01 Updates a policy LGDPDB01 Deletes a policy LGAPVS01 The VSAM program that LGAPDB01 calls when it adds a policy LGPOLVAL The new validation service, which does not yet exist. Bob creates it in section vi

The module is deliberately structured. Sections iv and v are analysis only: Bob reads the code and produces documentation, and no source file is modified until the rules and their dependencies have been established. The refactoring itself begins in section vi.

docs.title: ii. Why this matters
docs.text:
Refactoring a monolithic application is rarely as simple as cutting code out of one program and pasting it into another. The same rule is often written slightly differently in each place it appears, and the surrounding programs may depend on it in ways that were never documented.

Agentic AI is well suited to this work because it:

  • Locates the rules in the source code and records where each one lives, down to the program and line number
  • Maps the dependencies before any code is moved, including calling programs, Db2 tables and shared copybooks
  • Produces documentation and test cases as part of the work, rather than leaving them for later
  • Keeps the human in the loop: every file change is presented for your review and approval before it is applied
TASK WITH: Manual Analysis WITH: IBM Bob Premium Package for Z Business rules Read out of each program by hand Documented from the source, with program and line references Dependency mapping Cross-referencing programs, tables, and copybooks One mapping document with a dependency graph and diagrams Shared service Written by hand and documented afterwards Generated together with its documentation and test cases Integration Each calling program edited and checked separately Each edit proposed as a diff that you approve

docs.title: iii. Retrieve the GenApp lab files
docs.text:
This module introduces a second application. GenApp is the CICS general insurance sample application published by the IBM CICS development team on GitHub, and its policy programs contain the duplicated validation logic that this module consolidates. The retrieval follows the same procedure you used for the CBSA files during Registration and setup: Bob, in Agent mode, performs a sparse git clone on your behalf.

  1. Create a dedicated workspace folder for GenApp.

    • From the menu bar, select File › Open Folder... and click New folder.
    • Name the folder Bob PPZ L3 GenApp and select it to open it as your workspace.

    If the Welcome to IBM Z Open Editor in IBM Bob and Welcome to IBM Bob Premium Package for Z tabs open again, close them by clicking the X button on each tab.

    This is the same procedure you followed to create the Bob PPZ L3 workspace during setup.

    WHY A SEPARATE WORKSPACE?

    Z Code mode draws its answers from a scanned metadata database of the application in the current workspace, and the workspace rules you created during setup identify CBSA as the application in scope. Giving GenApp a workspace of its own keeps both the scan and the rules scoped to a single application.

  1. Near the bottom of the Agentic Sidebar, confirm that the Mode toggle reads Agent.

    Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar and press Enter (or click the send button) to submit it:

    Retrieve the sub-directory named "base" from the GitHub repository https://github.com/cicsdev/cics-genapp.git and place it in the current workspace folder. Then remove any temporary working directory you would have created.

    The base sub-directory holds the GenApp COBOL programs and copybooks under base/src/, along with the JCL and Db2 definitions that Bob consults when it maps the dependencies later in this module.

  1. Bob plans its approach and pauses at the Tools awaiting approval checkpoint before running any shell command.

    • Click Approve for task.
    • Bob clones the repository into a temporary directory, pauses for a second approval before copying base into the workspace, and then removes the temporary directory.
    • Approve the second request in the same way.

  1. When Bob reports that the task is complete, expand base › src in the Explorer tab and confirm that the folder contains the GenApp programs and copybooks.

    Confirm that the four programs this module works with are present:

    • lgapdb01.cbl
    • lgupdb01.cbl
    • lgdpdb01.cbl
    • lgapvs01.cbl

    The lgcmarea.cpy and lgpolicy.cpy copybooks should be present as well.

    WHY USE LOWER-CASE FILE NAMES?

    The repository stores its source files in lower case, so the program LGAPDB01 is found in the file base/src/lgapdb01.cbl. This module refers to programs by their upper-case names, which is also how Bob refers to them in its reports.

docs.title: iv. Identifying the business rules
docs.text:
Before any logic can be moved, it has to be identified. In this section Bob reads the three Db2 policy programs and documents every validation rule it finds within them.

  1. Near the bottom of the Agentic Sidebar, click the Mode toggle (which currently reads Agent) to expand the list of available modes.

  1. Select Z Code from the list.

    WHY Z CODE MODE?

    Z Code mode specializes in explaining, modifying and modernizing mainframe application code. It works at the level of programs, paragraphs, copybooks and CICS commands. You will remain in this mode for the remainder of the module.

  1. Copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar session window:

    Analyze LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01, and LGUPDB01. Identify all policy validation business rules including policy number format checks, policy type validation, and customer-policy relationship verification.

    With the prompt entered, hit Enter or press the Send button to the right of the chat interface.

  1. Bob begins the task by checking whether a scanned metadata database of the application already exists in the workspace. To follow the plan Bob has set for itself, click the to-do list icon at the top right of the Agentic Sidebar.

    IF BOB ASKS ABOUT SCANNING THE APPLICATION

    If no scanned database exists yet, Bob will ask whether to scan the application before proceeding with the analysis. Select Yes, scan the application now. When asked which language to scan, select COBOL. The analysis continues automatically once the scan completes.

    APPROVING TOOL REQUESTS

    Depending on your auto-approve settings, Bob may ask permission before it reads files or uses a tool. Click Approve for each request as it appears.

  1. Bob drafts a to-do list of seven items and works through them in sequence, checking each one off as it finishes. Notice the order of the list: Bob gathers context before it reads the code, and reads the code before it analyzes anything.

    # TASK OBJECTIVES 1 Read .bobz/local-settings.json to confirm database location Checks whether a scanned database of the application already exists 2 Scan application with scan_program tool Builds that database so it can answer from it 3 Invoke data-dictionary-management skill before reading COBOL files Checks whether a data dictionary exists that would give the field names business meaning 4 Read source files directly for analysis Reads the three programs and the copybooks they use 5 Assess Z Context needs and call z_context_tool if required Decides whether it needs more context about the z/OS environment before it answers 6 Analyze policy validation business rules across LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01, and LGUPDB01 The analysis the prompt requested 7 Deliver structured findings report Writes up the findings in the chat

  1. When all tasks are completed, Bob posts its report in the chat. The report opens with a Program Architecture Overview that places the three programs in context. Each is the database tier of a CICS LINK chain.

    It is called by one of the business-logic programs (LGAPOL01, LGDPOL01 or LGUPOL01) and in turn calls one of the VSAM-tier programs (LGAPVS01, LGDPVS01 or LGUPVS01).

    All three share the LGCMAREA copybook as their COMMAREA contract, and the policy-specific column lengths are defined in LGPOLICY.

    Below the overview, the rules are grouped by category. Each rule is assigned an ID and lists the programs it applies to, the condition that triggers it and the resulting outcome.

    The first category, the COMMAREA presence check, illustrates the format:

    • BR-01: a COMMAREA must be present. If EIBCALEN = 0, the program abends with code LGCA and the whole unit of work is rolled back
    • BR-02: the COMMAREA must meet the minimum header length. If EIBCALEN < 28, the program returns CA-RETURN-CODE = '98' and exits cleanly

  1. Scroll to the end of the report, which closes with a Return Code Summary, a list of Key Business Rule Gaps and a Summary of Findings. In the documented run, Bob identified 18 distinct business rules across 5 categories.

    The return code table summarizes how the three programs report problems:

    Code Meaning Programs that return it 00 Success All 01 Policy not found LGUPDB01 02 Optimistic lock failure, timestamps do not match LGUPDB01 70 Customer does not exist LGAPDB01 90 Generic DB2 error All 98 COMMAREA too short for the requested operation All 99 Unrecognised or unsupported request ID All

    The gaps deserve particular attention, since they describe conditions that the code does not check. Bob found three in the documented run. The programs do not validate against duplicate policies on add, and they perform no explicit date validation. There is also a case-sensitivity gap: LGDPOL01 uppercases the request ID before calling LGDPDB01, whereas a lowercase ID sent directly to LGDPDB01 is rejected with return code 99.

    RESPONSES MAY VARY

    Due to the nature of generative AI, the wording of Bob's report will differ from the screenshots. The number of rules, their IDs and the categories they are sorted into may not match either. Before continuing, confirm that the report addresses each element of the prompt:

    • Rules from all three programs: LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01 and LGUPDB01
    • The policy number format checks
    • The policy type validation
    • The customer-policy relationship verification

docs.title: v. Checking the dependencies
docs.text:
With the rules documented, the next step is to establish what else touches these programs before any logic is moved. That means the programs that call them, the Db2 tables they read and write, and the copybooks they share. Each of these can be affected by the refactoring.

The prompt for this section has four parts, and Bob addresses each in turn:

What the prompt asks What Bob does Map all programs that perform policy validation Identifies every program in which the request ID is inspected, the COMMAREA length is checked or a business rule is enforced. This extends beyond the three Db2 programs into the business-logic tier above them Check which programs call these validators Traces the CICS LINK chain from the screen programs at the top, through the business-logic programs, down to the Db2 and VSAM tiers Check which DB2 tables are accessed Builds a matrix of tables against programs, with the SQL operation each program performs on each table Identify shared copybooks Lists each copybook, its purpose and every program that includes it

Because this prompt is a follow-up within the same task, Bob builds on the findings of the first report rather than starting over. It also renders its diagrams as images and opens them in the editor as it works.

  1. With Z Code mode still active, copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar session window. The previous report should still be visible above the input field; this prompt builds on it, so do not start a new task.

    Map all programs that perform policy validation. Check which programs call these validators and which DB2 tables are accessed. Identify shared copybooks.

    Hit Enter or press the Send button.

    THE REPORT IS GENERATED IN STAGES

    This report is lengthy and Bob reports it one section at a time. While Bob is still writing, the status beneath the chat reads Still on it... as it works.

    Wait until the input field reads Follow up or start new task before scrolling to the summary at the end.

  1. The report opens with a legend for the program names, followed by the three-tier architecture of the policy validation chain: every policy change passes through a business-logic program, a Db2 program and a VSAM program before it completes. Beneath the diagram, the Programs That Perform Policy Validation table lists every program that performs validation. Each row records the program's tier and operations.

    The table that Bob generates provides answers to the first part of the previous prompt. In the documented run (screenshot below) it includes details on:

    • The four business-logic programs: LGIPOL01, LGAPOL01, LGDPOL01 and LGUPOL01. These verify that the COMMAREA is present and of sufficient length before any other processing takes place. LGDPOL01 additionally uppercases the request ID, and LGUPOL01 checks the length per policy type
    • The Db2 programs: LGAPDB01 relies on a Db2 foreign key to confirm that the customer exists, and LGIPDB01 confirms that the customer and policy match by means of a JOIN

  1. Scroll to DB2 Tables Accessed Per Program, which answers the third part of the prompt. The matrix has one row per table and one column per Db2 program, and each cell shows the SQL operation that program performs against that table.

    Three observations follow from this matrix:

    • Every program accesses POLICY, and each uses it differently. LGIPDB01 joins against it, while LGAPDB01 inserts into it and reads the timestamp back. LGDPDB01 deletes from it, and LGUPDB01 updates it through a cursor
    • The policy-type tables cascade on delete. LGDPDB01 deletes only from POLICY; the corresponding ENDOWMENT, HOUSE, MOTOR and COMMERCIAL rows are removed by a foreign-key constraint rather than by program code
    • COMMERCIAL policies cannot be updated. LGUPDB01 has no code path for them, which corresponds to one of the gaps Bob reported in the previous section

    Beneath the matrix, Key SQL Patterns by Program describes how each program interacts with Db2. LGIPDB01 uses four different SELECT strategies for commercial policies alone; LGAPDB01 inserts in two phases and reads the generated policy number back in between; and LGUPDB01 locks the row with a cursor before updating it.

  1. Continue to Shared Copybooks Across the Policy Validation Chain, where Bob draws the copybook dependencies as a diagram and then lists them in the Copybook Usage Matrix, recording the purpose of each copybook and the programs that include it.

    Copybook Purpose Used by LGCMAREA.cpy The COMMAREA contract shared by every request and response 21 programs, including every program in the policy chain LGPOLICY.cpy Db2 host variable structures and the policy-type length constants 9 programs, including all four Db2 programs SQLCA The Db2 SQL communications area 8 programs, every one that runs SQL SSMAP BMS map field definitions for the terminal screens The five screen programs, LGTESTP1 to LGTESTP4 and LGTESTC1

    LGCMAREA is the copybook that matters most for the next section. Two of its fields pass through every tier: CA-REQUEST-ID routes the request and gates the validation, and CA-RETURN-CODE carries the result back to the caller. Whatever the new service needs from the COMMAREA will have to be read through this copybook, in the same way the existing programs read it.

  1. The report concludes with a Policy Validation Program Map: a single diagram that ties the entire chain together, running from the four screen programs on the left through the business-logic and Db2 tiers to the VSAM programs on the right. The shared copybooks appear across the top, and a summary table beneath the diagram counts the programs by role.

    Role Count Programs Policy validators, all tiers 8 LGIPOL01, LGAPOL01, LGDPOL01, LGUPOL01, LGIPDB01, LGAPDB01, LGDPDB01, LGUPDB01 Screen programs that call the validators 4 LGTESTP1 to LGTESTP4 VSAM programs downstream 3 LGAPVS01, LGDPVS01, LGUPVS01 Shared error logger 1 LGSTSQ Statistics and event processor 1 LGASTAT1

    Above the map, Bob notes that LGPOLICY serves two purposes in a single file: it holds the length constants that the business-logic programs use to validate the COMMAREA, together with the Db2 host variable structures that the Db2 programs use as SELECT targets. Details of this kind determine where a shared service must draw its definitions from.

    RESPONSES MAY VARY

    As with the first report, Bob may order the sections differently or draw the diagrams another way, and the counts in the summary table can shift by a program or two from one run to the next. Before continuing, confirm that the report addresses each element of the prompt:

    • Every program that performs policy validation, beyond the three Db2 programs you began with
    • The programs that call them, from the screen programs downward
    • The Db2 tables each program accesses, and the operations performed
    • The shared copybooks, and the programs that include each one

docs.title: vi. Creating the validation service
docs.text:
This section is the first in which source code is written. Bob creates a new COBOL program, LGPOLVAL, and moves the validation logic out of the existing programs and into it.

The prompt has two parts. In the documented run, Bob addressed both and then took one additional step on its own initiative:

What the prompt asks What Bob does Create LGPOLVAL service that consolidates policy validation rules Writes the new LGPOLVAL program together with a LGPOLVAL.cpy copybook that defines the COMMAREA through which callers communicate with the service Extract validation logic from LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01, LGAPVS01 and LGUPDB01 Takes each rule identified in section iv, records its origin and implements it as a check inside the service Not requested until section vii Updates the three Db2 programs to call the service, so that the extracted logic does not remain active in two places

Because this prompt is a follow-up within the same task, Bob already holds the rules and dependencies from the two previous reports and uses them to decide what belongs in the service and what the calling programs retain.

  1. With Z Code mode still active, copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar session window. The dependency report from the previous section should still be visible above the input field.

    Create LGPOLVAL service that consolidates policy validation rules. Extract validation logic from LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01, LGAPVS01 and LGUPDB01 into the new service.

    Hit Enter or press the Send button to execute the instruction.

    This prompt takes noticeably longer than the previous two, since Bob is now writing and editing code rather than reading it.

  1. Bob reports its results under the heading LGPOLVAL Service — Refactoring Delivery, beginning with the files it created and the files it modified. The Explorer tab reflects the same outcome: the two new files are marked U and the three edited programs are marked M, while the footer of the chat reads 5 files changed.

    File What happened base/src/lgpolval.cbl Created. The new validation service, 304 lines base/src/lgpolval.cpy Created. The COMMAREA copybook that callers use to communicate with the service, 27 lines base/src/lgapdb01.cbl Modified. Gained a WS-VALCA area from the new copybook and a LINK to LGPOLVAL ahead of its policy-type EVALUATE base/src/lgdpdb01.cbl Modified. Its IF/ELSE guard on the request ID is replaced by the LINK, and the logic the service now owns is removed base/src/lgupdb01.cbl Modified. The LINK replaces the inline type-routing block

    The Undo all and Show all controls beside the file count allow you to roll back every change or review them individually. Leave them untouched for now; you will review the changes in Section vii.

  1. Scroll to What Was Extracted Into LGPOLVAL. This table is central to the report: each row pairs one rule with the program it was extracted from and the check inside the service that now enforces it.

    The table contains two kinds of rule:

    • Rules that were explicitly coded, such as the request ID prefix check and the policy type checks for add, delete and update. Each existed in a slightly different form in each program (an inline IF in LGDPDB01 and an EVALUATE with a WHEN OTHER branch in the other two) and each is now a single check within the service
    • Rules that were only implied. None of the three programs verified that the customer number was non-zero or that a policy number had been supplied; each relied on Db2 to reject the request later. Bob implemented both as explicit checks that run before any Db2 work takes place

    Beneath the table, the LGPOLVAL COMMAREA Interface documents the contract defined in LGPOLVAL.cpy. A caller supplies an operation code, the request ID and the customer and policy numbers, and receives a result code and a readable reason in return:

    Field Picture Purpose VCA-OPCODE X(2) Which operation is being validated: AP, AV, DP, UP, or IP VCA-REQUEST-ID X(6) Copied from the caller's CA-REQUEST-ID VCA-CUSTOMER-NUM 9(10) Copied from CA-CUSTOMER-NUM VCA-POLICY-NUM 9(10) Copied from CA-POLICY-NUM, zero for an add VCA-RESULT-CODE 9(2) 00 for pass, 10 to 50 for the check that failed VCA-RESULT-MSG X(40) A human-readable reason for the result

  1. The report closes with the Return Code Mapping and a diagram of the Architecture After Refactoring. The mapping is what keeps the change invisible to the programs upstream: each service result code is translated back into the CA-RETURN-CODE value that the caller has always returned, so the screen programs observe no difference.

    Service result Meaning Caller returns 00 All checks passed Carries on with its Db2 work 10 COMMAREA too short 98 20 Unrecognised prefix or opcode 99 30 Policy type not supported 99 40 Customer number is zero 98 50 Policy number required but zero 98

    The diagram illustrates the refactored chain. Each Db2 program links to LGPOLVAL with its own opcode; on a result of 00 the caller proceeds, and on any other result it sets CA-RETURN-CODE and returns without touching Db2.

    The explanation beneath the diagram accounts for the one program named in the prompt that was not wired to the service. Bob assigned LGAPVS01 an AV opcode in the service but did not add a LINK to it, because LGAPDB01 only reaches LGAPVS01 after validation has already passed; validating again in the VSAM tier would check the same request twice.

    RESPONSES MAY VARY

    Bob's delivery will differ from the documented run in its details: the names of the checks, the opcodes and the result code values may not match the screenshots, and Bob may or may not wire the calling programs in this step. Before continuing, confirm that the delivery includes:

    • lgpolval.cbl and lgpolval.cpy in base/src
    • Every rule from section iv in the What Was Extracted table, each with a corresponding check in the service
    • A mapping from each service result code back to a CA-RETURN-CODE value
    • An explanation of what was done with LGAPVS01, and why

    BOB HAS ALREADY STARTED ON THE NEXT SECTION

    The prompt in section vii asks Bob to update the programs to call LGPOLVAL and to add error handling for a failed call. In the documented run, Bob had already wired the three Db2 programs to the service during this step, leaving less for section vii to do than the prompt implies.

docs.title: vii. Adding the link code to the main programs
docs.text:
The service now exists, and the three Db2 programs already call it. This section asks Bob to complete the integration: ensure that every program named in the prompt uses the service in place of its own validation, and add error handling for the case in which the call to the service fails.

The prompt has three parts, and Bob reviews the current state of the code before acting on any of them:

What the prompt asks What Bob does Update LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01, LGAPVS01 and LGUPDB01 to call LGPOLVAL Reads all four programs in their current state, confirms which already link to the service and adds the call to the one that does not (LGAPVS01) Replace inline validation with CICS LINK calls Identifies checks that remain duplicated in the callers now that the service owns them, and removes them Add proper error handling for service failures Adds RESP and RESP2 to every LINK to the service, and gives the callers a means of reporting that the service itself could not be reached

  1. With Z Code mode still active, copy and paste the following prompt into the Agentic Sidebar session window. The delivery report from the previous section should still be visible above the input field.

    Update LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01, LGAPVS01 and LGUPDB01 to call LGPOLVAL service. Replace inline validation with CICS LINK calls. Add proper error handling for service failures.

    Hit Enter or press the Send button.

  1. Bob begins by reading the four programs in their current state and writing up a gap analysis, one program at a time, before it changes a single line.

    This is the same plan-first discipline you practiced in Module 2: Bob first establishes what has already been done and what remains outstanding.

    Program What Bob found What it decided to do LGDPDB01 The LINK is in place and the former IF/ELSE request ID check has been removed. The EIBCALEN < 28 guard remains, which Bob retains as an initial safeguard Add RESP handling to the LINK LGAPDB01 The LINK is in place, but the EVALUATE retains a WHEN OTHER branch that duplicates a check the service now performs. The length calculation that INSERT-ENDOW depends on also lacks its starting value Remove the duplicate branch, add RESP handling and move the ADD WS-CA-HEADER-LEN statement ahead of the type EVALUATE LGUPDB01 The LINK is in place, and the per-type length checks are already handled upstream Add RESP handling to the LINK LGAPVS01 No call to the service yet Full integration: a WS-VALCA area and an EIBCALEN guard, the LINK with the AV opcode and a result check before the VSAM write

    At the bottom of the analysis, Bob condenses this into three items of work: RESP/RESP2 handling on all three Db2 programs, the length fix in LGAPDB01 and the full integration of LGAPVS01.

  1. When the edits are complete, Bob reports under Changes Delivered — LGPOLVAL Integration, with one table per file and a line number for every change. The footer of the chat now reads 6 files changed rather than five, since LGAPVS01 has been added to the list.

    LGDPDB01 illustrates the pattern that the other two Db2 programs follow:

    # Change What it is for 1 WS-RESP and WS-RESP2 added to Working-Storage Storage for the response from the LINK 2 INITIALIZE WS-VALCA before the MOVEs Starts the service COMMAREA from a clean state on every call 3 RESP(WS-RESP) RESP2(WS-RESP2) on the LINK Asks CICS to report the outcome of the LINK instead of abending 4 A LINK failure check: if WS-RESP is not DFHRESP(NORMAL), set CA-RETURN-CODE to 95, log the condition and return The error handling the prompt requested 5 Column spacing aligned on the MOVE-to-WS-VALCA statements Cosmetic alignment, so that the block matches the surrounding code

  1. Scroll on, and the same five changes appear for LGAPDB01 and LGUPDB01 at their own line numbers. LGAPDB01 receives two additional changes: its result-code check now treats both 20 (bad opcode) and 30 (bad type) as return code 99, and the ADD WS-CA-HEADER-LEN TO WS-REQUIRED-CA-LEN statement has been moved ahead of the type EVALUATE, where INSERT-ENDOW requires it for its length calculation.

  1. The final table covers LGAPVS01, marked new integration. It is the largest change in this step, because the program is being connected to the service for the first time. Beneath it, Error Code Additions lists the two return codes introduced in this section.

    # Change in LGAPVS01 What it is for 1 WS-RESP and WS-RESP2 initialised to zero As in the Db2 programs 2 WS-VALCA group added with COPY LGPOLVAL The service COMMAREA 3 An EIBCALEN = 0 abend guard, LGCA The same initial check the Db2 programs perform 4 The full LINK block with opcode AV and RESP/RESP2 handling The call to the service 5 LINK failure sets CA-RETURN-CODE to 82, logs it, and returns Kept distinct from 80, which already denotes a VSAM write failure 6 A validation failure returns 99 for a bad type or opcode and 98 for anything else Maps the service result back to the codes callers already understand New code Meaning Returned by 95 The LINK to LGPOLVAL failed, for example because the program is not installed LGDPDB01, LGAPDB01, LGUPDB01 82 The same condition, reported from the VSAM tier LGAPVS01

    Both codes are deliberately distinct from those already in use: 80 (VSAM write), 90 (Db2 error), 98 (short COMMAREA) and 99 (bad request ID). A caller can therefore distinguish a failure to reach the service from a problem with the data itself.

  1. Bob closes with an Execution Flow After Changes diagram that follows a single request through a refactored program. The EIBCALEN guards are evaluated first, followed by the LINK to LGPOLVAL and then one of three exits. A bad RESP returns 95 or 82, a failed check returns 98 or 99, and a successful validation proceeds to the Db2 or VSAM work.

    REVIEWING THE CHANGES FILE BY FILE

    To review the changes themselves, locate the bar directly above the chat input. It reads 6 files changed, with Undo all and Show all controls on the right. Click Show all.

    The bar expands into a list of every file Bob modified, showing the number of lines added and removed in each. In the documented run, lgpolval.cbl consists entirely of additions, while lgdpdb01.cbl shows the most removals because it contained the most inline validation. Click a file name to open it.

    The file opens in a diff view titled Bob Edit of, with every line Bob added highlighted in green. In the case of lgpolval.cbl that is the entire program. Take a moment to review the comment block at the top. It names the four programs the logic was extracted from and the 70-byte COMMAREA defined by LGPOLVAL.cpy, and it documents the five opcodes and the meaning of each result code.

    RESPONSES MAY VARY

    The line numbers, the exact return code values and the amount of work already completed in the previous section may not match the screenshots. Before continuing, confirm that:

    • All four programs, including LGAPVS01, call LGPOLVAL through a CICS LINK in place of their own validation
    • Every LINK carries RESP and RESP2, and a bad response sets a return code and exits cleanly
    • The new return codes do not collide with those the programs already used
    • The 6 files changed bar lists the service, its copybook and the four programs

    COMPILE, DEFINE, AND TEST BEFORE USE

    Everything Bob has done in this module is a source change within your workspace. Before the change could be put to use, LGPOLVAL would need to be compiled and defined to CICS, and the refactored programs recompiled and tested. None of those steps are part of this lab.

docs.title: viii. Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Bob documented the validation rules and mapped their dependencies before any code was changed
  • Each rule was traced back to the program and the lines it came from
  • The validation logic formerly repeated across the policy programs now resides in a single service, LGPOLVAL
  • The original programs reach the service through a CICS LINK and handle a failed call themselves
  • Every file change was presented as a diff for your approval before it was applied
  • Each section produced a report in the chat, so the refactoring is documented as well as implemented
  • A refactored program still has to be compiled, deployed and tested before the change is complete

This concludes the hands-on lab. The four reports remain in your chat history and the refactored programs remain in your workspace, so you can return to any section at your convenience.

In order to receive credit for completion of this course, you must perform one of the two actions (in accordance with your role) described below:

IBMers: RECORD A STAND & DELIVER

IBM regular employees must record a Stand & Deliver to receive credit for this course. By default, IBMers will be evaluated by their First Line Manager (FLM) — although they may request another manager to evaluate their Stand & Deliver, if appropriate. Instructions on how to submit a Stand & Deliver are included within the activity on IBM YourLearning.

Business Partners: COMPLETE THE SKILLS EVALUATION QUIZ

The skills evaluation quiz only applies to business partners. The quiz consists of multiple choice questions, with four possible responses (and only one correct answer) for each question. The quiz questions will ask you about on-screen text or descriptions that come up as you work through the lab guide. Participants must pass the quiz with a grade of 80% or higher. Answers to the quiz can only be determined by carefully following the instructions of the hands-on lab. A link is provided within the course page on IBM Training.
